title: Legal Research and Citation
description: Plan legal research, locate and compare primary sources, check authority and currency, and create traceable citations and research logs. Third course in the J.D. Preparation pathway; includes an original, self-contained research packet.
author: Erudior
disclaimer: Independent educational preparation only; not legal advice, university credit, a J.D. degree, or a determination of bar eligibility. All Larch and Maren materials are fictional. Exercises use a fixed teaching snapshot; real matters require current jurisdiction-specific research.

lessons.title: Turn a problem into a research plan
lessons.body:
## Research starts before the search box

A case-reading course teaches you to understand an opinion already in front of you.
Research adds a different problem: deciding which documents you need, locating them,
and explaining how far your investigation supports a conclusion. A persuasive-looking
result can be irrelevant to your forum, superseded, or based on a different statutory
version. Finding a sentence that sounds useful is only the beginning.

A **[[research plan]]** is a written account of the question, scope, available sources and
next actions. It need not be long. Its purpose is to prevent aimless searching and
make your assumptions visible. This course uses an original fictional Larch packet
so that every required exercise can be completed offline. Open the Larch research
packet reference. Its dates and institutions are invented; do not search for these
cases on the public web or treat them as legal authority outside the exercise.

## Define the decision you need to support

An **[[issue statement]]** turns a story into a bounded question. “Research room law”
is too broad. “Which decision period applies to a complete town-room application
received June 25, Year 5?” identifies both the event and the legal issue. The
**[[forum]]** is the tribunal in which the question would be decided. Here P1 specifies
a Larch trial court. That matters because P2 defines which courts supply binding
holdings for that tribunal.

Record the **[[relevant date]]** of the event as well as the research date. Noor's
receipt date is June 25; the research snapshot is August 20. These dates do different
jobs. The first helps select the applicable law; the second tells another researcher
how current your inquiry intends to be. An amended statute may govern some new
applications without governing older ones still pending. A timestamp saying you
opened a page today cannot answer that transition question.

Separate established facts, assumptions and unknowns. The packet stipulates
completeness and delivery for the capstone. In a real assignment you might need to
request those facts. An **[[assumption]]** fills a gap provisionally; it must be labelled
and tested if it could change the analysis. Do not convert “I do not know when the
application arrived” into “it probably arrived before the amendment.”

## Map the work into answerable branches

A **[[research scope]]** describes the issues, jurisdictions, periods and collections
you will investigate. For the Larch problem, create branches for the statute and
amendment, implementing regulation, relevant cases, later treatment and unresolved
coverage. The plan should include potentially adverse sources. If you search only
for support for ten days, you may miss both Cedar's fifteen-day proposition and the
legislation introducing fourteen days.

A research budget allocates time or resources among those branches. Budgeting
does not guarantee completeness. It helps you decide which uncertainty to resolve
first and what to report if access runs out. Give priority to controlling text and
its transition rule before spending time reading a distant jurisdiction's analogous
case. Keep a place for promising leads without letting each new link replace the
assignment's central question.

Your **[[deliverable]]** is the product the assignment requires. Here it is an authority
table, research log and explanatory note. Those products require more than a list of
links. You need source identity, propositions, dates, treatment and reproducible
search steps. Start collecting that information while you work; reconstructing it
from memory later is unreliable. The Research workbench supplies reusable fields.

### Example 1: turn Noor's story into a plan

Noor says, “They took too long to answer my room request.” First identify the actor
and covered activity: the Town Room Office and a town-operated study room. Act section
1 establishes that this kind of application falls within the packet's scope.
Second, record receipt on June 25 and the decision sent July 8; do not use the date
of the requested room reservation to select the decision period.

Third, formulate the question: under the version applicable to a complete application
received June 25, was the July 8 decision timely? Fourth, list sources needed: Act
sections 2–4, Amendment A, Rule 8 and relevant cases. Fifth, reserve a separate line
for remedies. The assignment supplies no remedy rule, so even a late decision cannot
support an invented damages award. This plan is useful because each listed source
answers a specific question rather than merely adding reading volume.

### Example 2: distinguish a completed check from a planned check

A researcher writes, “Check all later cases through August 20.” The packet's case
index actually ends August 15. Rewrite the plan in two parts. Completed within this
exercise: read IDX1–IDX2 and the later authority they identify. Planned but unavailable:
search a current relevant court collection or citator for August 16–20 and assess
any pertinent material outside this index's coverage.

Do not write “current through August 20” merely because that is the desired date.
The plan's target and the source's coverage are different. The legislative change
register does cover August 20, but that does not extend the judicial index. A strong
handoff explains this exact gap so the next researcher knows what to do.

## Practice with feedback

Draft a four-line plan for Ivo's July 3 application: forum and issue; event and
research dates; first sources; unresolved coverage. Compare your draft with this
model: “Larch trial court; timely written decision on a complete application.
Receipt July 3, decision July 18, research snapshot August 20, Year 5. Start with
section 2 and A1, then Rule 8 and Birch. Case-index coverage ends August 15; later
judicial developments remain unchecked.” Your wording may differ if each distinction
is preserved.

Now change one fact: the application might omit the requested room. Add a branch
for Rule 8.1 and the missing fact. Do not count from the first contact until you know
when a complete application was received. This adjustment shows why planning is
iterative. New facts can change the question and the order of work without making
the original plan useless.

## Common mistakes

Starting with a conclusion encourages selective searching. Starting with every
possible legal issue makes the task unmanageable. Use the assigned issue, identify
what could change it, and state exclusions. Confusing a research date with a source
cutoff creates false assurance. Confusing a deadline rule with a remedy creates a
claim the sources never supported. Finally, do not record an intended search as
completed simply because you know how you would perform it.

## Key points

- State the forum, issue, relevant events and research date before searching.
- Separate supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
- Tie each source branch to a question and a deliverable.
- Keep completed work and unavailable follow-up visibly distinct.

lessons.title: Use secondary sources and improve a search
lessons.body:
## A helpful explanation is a starting point

A **[[secondary source]]** explains, organizes or comments on law without itself being
the relevant enacted text or judicial decision. Guides can introduce vocabulary,
identify issues and point you toward primary sources. This is valuable when you do
not yet know the terminology a statute or court uses. But usefulness as a guide does
not make commentary binding in the forum. The Larch packet deliberately includes
two editions of a guide that lead to different next steps.

A **[[primary source]]** is the lawmaking or adjudicative material itself, such as a
statute, regulation or opinion. Classification and authority are separate questions.
Cedar is a primary judicial source even though Birch overrules its fifteen-day
proposition. Elm is also primary, but its Maren court and statute do not govern the
Larch deadline. Start by classifying the source, then ask what it can establish.

## Read the source's credentials and boundaries

Check author, publisher, edition, date, subject and jurisdiction. **[[Source provenance]]**
is the account of where a document came from and who issued it. A clinic's name on
a guide does not turn it into a court opinion. A copy of an opinion on a private
website can still reproduce primary material, but you must verify identity, text
and status rather than infer them from an attractive page design.

An **[[edition]]** identifies a particular version of a work. G1 is January Year 5;
G2 is May Year 5. The January guide predates Birch. The May guide incorporates Birch
but predates Amendment A. Neither is automatically current for an August inquiry.
Publication dates help you identify what to update; they do not replace reading the
sources cited or checking developments after publication.

Treat a useful citation or keyword as a **[[research lead]]**: a direction to investigate,
not a conclusion already established. Read G2's reference to B2, then open Birch
and inspect its precise proposition. Following a lead should leave a record of what
you actually found. If the promised support is absent, log that mismatch and revise
the analysis. Do not keep the guide's conclusion merely because it was your first hit.

## Search words, fields and collections deliberately

A **[[search query]]** is the request submitted to a collection. Its meaning includes
the searched field and active filters, not just the words. “Study room” in case
titles is different from “complete application” across full text. A **[[search filter]]**
limits the collection by a property such as court, date or document type. Filters
help focus results, but an incorrect filter can hide the very authority you need.

Begin with ordinary language, then add statutory phrases and institutional names
found in reliable sources. Try variants of the concept without assuming every
service handles quotation marks, plurals or connectors identically. Consult that
service's search help when exact syntax matters. In our offline exercise, IDX1
stipulates results so that no platform account or live search is necessary.

A zero-result query means the specified search found nothing in its specified
collection. It does not establish that no law exists. Check spelling, fields,
filters, date coverage and alternate vocabulary before making a negative inference.
Record the unsuccessful attempt because it explains why your next query changed.
A log containing only successful searches can hide the boundaries of your method.

### Example 1: repair an unproductive query

You search case titles for “study room” and get zero results under IDX1. First state
the actual inference: no supplied caption matched that phrase in this index. Second,
inspect the packet's institutional vocabulary: the opinions use “Town Room Office.”
Third, revise the query to “complete application” in full text. IDX1 supplies three
hits: Rowan, Cedar and Birch.

Fourth, open those documents. A hit is not yet a relevant holding. Rowan concerns an
electronic decision, Cedar supports fifteen days, and Birch rejects that proposition.
Record the exact field change and which passages mattered. A weaker log saying
“searched online; found three cases” would not explain how the initial failure was
corrected or allow another researcher to reproduce it.

### Example 2: use two guide editions responsibly

G1 says fifteen days under Cedar. First record that G1 is commentary dated January
Year 5. Next open C2 to confirm that Cedar actually made that statement. Then search
for later treatment rather than stopping at confirmation. IDX2 directs you to B2,
where the higher court overrules that point.

G2 says Birch rejects fifteen days and directs you to the ten-day statute. That is
a better lead for Birch's rule, but it is still a May edition. Checking legislation
finds A1, which introduces fourteen days for applications received on or after July
1. The correct workflow preserves the useful parts of each lead while updating the
proposition. You do not simply choose whichever guide is newer and treat it as final.

## Practice with feedback

A classmate writes, “The May guide is the newest guide in our packet, so its ten-day
statement settles Ivo's July application.” Identify the missing step. Feedback:
check primary statutory text and amendments after the guide's publication, including
A1's receipt-date rule. Ivo's July 3 receipt falls into A1's fourteen-day category.
The guide's relative newness does not freeze legislation at May.

Next, label these items: the Act, G1 and M1. The Act is primary legislation. G1 is
secondary commentary. M1 is a nonbinding agency staff direction under P3, not an
amendment or a controlling interpretation. Agency material can have several forms;
read what the document is and the authority under which it was issued rather than
using its logo to decide its legal effect.

Finally, write a follow-up for a guide citation whose full text you cannot access.
A sound answer says the lead remains unverified, records the missing document and
explains how to obtain or replace it. It does not invent the holding from the title
or silently convert an inaccessible source into a completed review.

## Common mistakes

Equating “found on a government site” with “binding for this proposition” skips source
classification. Equating “published recently” with “fully updated” skips version and
treatment checks. Copying a summary's citation without opening the cited text risks
repeating somebody else's error. Searching only a single phrase in a single field
can turn a vocabulary mismatch into a false claim that the law is silent.

## Key points

- Use commentary to learn vocabulary and find primary-source leads.
- Record edition, provenance and jurisdiction before relying on an explanation.
- Change queries deliberately and log fields, filters and coverage.
- Update the cited primary sources even when the guide seems recent.

lessons.title: Find the applicable statute and regulation
lessons.body:
## The right words in the wrong version are still a problem

A statutory section may look like a complete answer because it is concise and comes
from an authoritative publisher. Yet the operative rule can depend on definitions,
amendments, effective dates and related sections. Read the section in its context
and identify which version governs the event. In the Larch packet, ten, fourteen
and fifteen days all appear in official-looking documents. Locating the numbers is
easy; explaining which one applies is the research task.

**[[Codification]]** organizes statutory law by subject in a code. A **[[session law]]**
is an enacted law as published in the sequence of enactments. These forms answer
related but different research needs: a subject arrangement helps find provisions,
while an enactment can disclose the precise change and its timing. Do not assume
that the current text displayed in a compilation answers every historical question.
Our packet supplies an original Act and a separate amendment so that the transition
is visible without requiring an outside database.

## Read amendments as instructions, not just new numbers

An **[[amendment]]** changes an existing legal text. First identify exactly what it
changes. Amendment A replaces ten with fourteen in section 2 for a defined class
of applications. A2 leaves sections 1, 3, 4 and 5 unchanged. It would be a mistake
to infer that the amendment also changes what counts as writing, permits longer
agency extensions, or creates a damages remedy.

An **[[effective date]]** is when a provision takes legal effect under its terms. It
may differ from the date of enactment. A was enacted June 10 but takes effect July
1, Year 5. More importantly, its **[[transition provision]]** tells you which events
receive the new rule. A1 uses receipt of a complete application on or after July 1.
The provision expressly preserves ten days for earlier receipts even if a deadline
falls in July. Read that full sentence before counting days.

Build a small event record: receipt, applicable version, day zero, counted days and
decision date. Counting cannot repair a version error. If you choose fourteen days
for Noor because the decision was sent in July, an impeccable calendar calculation
still applies the wrong rule. The date relevant to the transition is receipt, not
the date you research or the date the Office chooses to respond.

## Connect a regulation to its statutory authority

A **[[delegation]]** gives another institution authority to act within specified bounds.
A **[[regulation]]** is an agency rule; its legal effect requires attention to the
applicable legal system and its source of authority. For this exercise, P3 supplies
the hierarchy and Act section 4 permits application forms and identifying information
but forbids lengthening the decision period. That limit is part of the research,
not an optional policy consideration.

Rule 8.1 identifies completeness, and Rule 8.2 explains day zero. Rule 8.3 purports
to permit fifteen days. Compare it with section 4 and Birch B2 before using it. A
compiled regulation can remain visible after a court rejects its use. Textual
presence does not establish validity for every proposition. Record both that the
rule register shows no textual amendment and that judicial treatment changes how
8.3 may be used.

For real federal research, the Office of the Law Revision Counsel explains where
to inspect Code currency and classification information. The eCFR's own reader
aids explain the compilation's legal status and verification directions. Use those
publishers' current explanations rather than assuming that every government search
page is an official, fully current legal compilation. The Citation and currency
reference links the sources; the packet exercises require no live lookup.

### Example 1: a deadline crossing the amendment date

Noor's complete application arrives June 25. First apply A1's trigger: June 25 is
before July 1, so the original ten-day period applies. Second use P4 and Rule 8.2:
June 25 is day zero; June 26 is day one. Third count through June 30, day five,
and continue through July 5, day ten. The statutory deadline is July 5.

The Office sends its decision July 8, day thirteen. Within the supplied materials,
that is late. The crossing into July does not restart the clock or switch the period
to fourteen days. Section 5 separately prevents an inference that silence approved
the application. Your research note should cite both the original section 2 and A1,
because the transition provision explains why the older number remains applicable.

### Example 2: a rule that cannot lengthen the statute

Ivo's complete application arrives July 3. A1 selects fourteen days. July 4 is day
one and July 17 is day fourteen. The Office invokes Rule 8.3 and sends a paper
decision July 18, day fifteen.

Trace the claimed authority rather than accepting the agency's preferred number.
Section 4 forbids a rule from lengthening section 2. Birch B2 rejects 8.3's fifteen-day
proposition under the earlier ten-day text; A1 now sets fourteen but leaves section
4 unchanged. Nothing supplied revives a fifteen-day allowance. Explain both the
current statutory text and the continuing delegation limit. Paper form does not
cure a late decision, just as an electronic form does not itself make one late.

## Practice with feedback

An application is received June 30. Which period applies if its deadline is in July?
Feedback: ten days, because A1 selects by receipt date and preserves the earlier
period. Under P4, July 1 is day one and July 10 is day ten. Do not use the date of
the eventual deadline as the transition trigger.

Now suppose a researcher cites M1's instruction to use fourteen days for every
pending application. Identify the source conflict. Feedback: M1 is nonbinding staff
guidance; it uses pending status instead of A1's receipt-date boundary. Read A1 as
the controlling transition text under P3. Record M1 as a rejected lead so a reviewer
can see that you encountered and resolved the inconsistency.

## Common mistakes

Reading only a section heading can hide definitions and transition language. Using
the enactment date as the effective date ignores the law's own timing. Treating
unchanged regulatory text as unaffected authority ignores judicial treatment.
Finally, do not import real-world counting rules into this fictional exercise. P4
expressly supplies the calculation rules; a real matter would require researching
the relevant jurisdiction's actual time-computation and service provisions.

## Key points

- Locate both the operative text and the provisions choosing its application.
- Separate enactment, effectiveness, receipt and research dates.
- Read a regulation with its delegation and later judicial treatment.
- State what the sources establish without inventing a remedy.

lessons.title: Locate cases and verify the passage you need
lessons.body:
## Retrieval is not interpretation

Finding a case with the right keywords does not show that the court adopted the
proposition you want. You must identify the document, understand the court's task
and locate the relevant language in its context. This lesson connects the earlier
Case Reading course to research: read enough of each retrieved source to decide
whether it answers your issue and what further checking it requires.

A **[[caption]]** identifies a case by its named parties. It is useful for retrieval,
but it does not establish the governing issue or the result by itself. In IDX1,
searching for “study room” in captions misses all three Larch cases even though each
concerns room applications. Their captions name the Town Room Office. The failure
illustrates a field mismatch, not the absence of relevant law.

## Identify the court's task and voice

**[[Procedural posture]]** describes how the dispute reached the deciding court and
what ruling it is reviewing. Rowan reverses a trial court's objection to electronic
form. Birch reverses a timeliness ruling and remands. A remand is not a damages award.
If you retrieve only a sentence announcing reversal, you still need to know which
ruling was reversed and what remained unresolved.

An **[[opinion type]]** identifies the kind of judicial writing, such as a majority,
concurrence or dissent. P2 makes published majority holdings relevant to binding
force in this packet. A search excerpt that does not identify its speaker cannot
be assumed to state the court's governing rule. Our supplied opinions are expressly
labelled published majorities so the exercise can focus on the next distinctions.
Real searches require verifying those labels rather than assuming them.

A **[[holding]]** is a proposition the court decides as necessary to its resolution of
the issue before it. A **[[dictum]]** is judicial language beyond what is necessary to
that decision. Classifying a statement requires context and can itself involve
argument. Avoid treating the most general sentence as the holding simply because
it is easy to quote. Rowan R2 resolves the specified savable message; R3 explicitly
leaves unsavable messages and late-decision remedies open.

## Read the source instead of the search wrapper

An **[[editorial summary]]** is a publisher's description of a case. It can point to an
issue, but it is not judicial language merely because it appears beside an opinion.
H1 intentionally says that electronic messages always satisfy writing requirements.
R2–R3 support a narrower result about the savable message at issue and reserve an
unsavable-message question. Attribute the claim to the source that actually made it.

A **[[pinpoint locator]]** identifies the specific part of a source supporting a
proposition. Here the stable paragraph labels R2 or B2 serve that purpose. A citation
to the entire packet makes a reader hunt through unrelated sources. A precise
locator both helps retrieval and forces you to check that the cited passage really
supports the sentence. In a real document, the appropriate locator may be a page,
paragraph, section or other unit required by the applicable citation convention.

Keep the source's pagination or paragraph system separate from a viewer's screen
position. “PDF page 3” may be a cover page or a differently numbered page. Preserve
the official or otherwise appropriate locator while noting the local file and
version in your research log. Do not invent a reporter citation when the source
provides only a slip opinion or another supported form.

### Example 1: test a broad electronic-message claim

A draft says, “Rowan proves that any electronic message is legally sufficient.”
First find the decisive passage: R2 refers to section 3 and a savable message.
Second read the facts: delivery and completeness are agreed in R1. Third read the
reservation in R3: the court does not decide the unsavable-message situation.

Rewrite the claim: “Under the packet's section 3, Rowan accepted the delivered,
savable electronic decision before it; it left unsavable messages unresolved.”
Cite R1–R3 as needed, with R2 for the central holding and R3 for the limitation.
The word “savable” is legally significant because the statute uses it and the court
relies on it. Omitting it would broaden the proposition beyond the supplied support.

### Example 2: distinguish what Cedar said from what governs now

C2 plainly endorses a fifteen-day period. It would be inaccurate to rewrite Cedar
as if it originally required ten days. Research preserves what the historical case
said while separately recording later treatment. First identify C2 as the original
supporting passage. Then use IDX2 to locate Birch B2, which overrules that point.

The resulting entry says: “Cedar adopted the fifteen-day reading; Birch later
rejected it.” Cedar may be useful for explaining a legal development, but it cannot
supply the operative fifteen-day rule in the packet's later snapshot. B3 also
reserves remedies, so Birch's reversal does not let you promise a particular award.
Source identity, proposition, later treatment and disposition belong in separate
fields because each answers a different question.

## Practice with feedback

Which passage best supports the statement that Birch leaves Rowan's electronic-message
holding undisturbed? Feedback: B3 expressly says so. R2 establishes the original
holding; B3 establishes the later court's treatment of it. A citation to C3 only
shows that Cedar did not discuss electronic form. Silence in one case is not the
same as an express statement in another.

Now compare “Rowan, R2” with “search results, first hit.” The former locates a stable
source passage in this exercise; the latter depends on a changing display and does
not identify the source. A good research note can include both the search step and
the stable source citation, but they serve different purposes. The search record
explains discovery; the citation supports the legal proposition.

Finally, test the claim “Birch awarded a room to the applicant.” Feedback: B3 reverses
and remands the timeliness ruling and does not decide a remedy. Neither the case
nor section 5 supports the claim. An outcome word such as “reversed” must be read
with its object and the relief actually ordered.

## Common mistakes

Do not attribute a guide, headnote or search excerpt to a judge without checking
the opinion. Do not confuse a party's contention with an adopted holding. Do not
use an exact quotation as a substitute for understanding its limiting context.
And do not erase historical propositions when updating a case; explain how later
sources change their permissible use.

## Key points

- Verify court, opinion type, posture and precise proposition after retrieval.
- Use the opinion's text to check editorial summaries.
- Record stable pinpoint locators and source versions.
- Keep original holdings and later treatment distinct.

lessons.title: Update authority and disclose coverage gaps
lessons.body:
## Updating is a chain of supported checks

A **[[currency check]]** investigates changes or later treatment that may affect a
source's use for your question. It is not satisfied by noting the date you opened
the document. An old opinion can remain important, a recently accessed guide can
be outdated, and a newly amended statute can preserve the old rule for earlier
events. Updating connects the source, the proposition, the relevant date and the
coverage of the tools you actually used.

Keep legislative, regulatory and judicial checks separate. AR1 covers legislative
changes through August 20. The Rule 8 register covers textual amendments through
the same date. IDX1–IDX2 cover specified published Larch opinions only through
August 15. Combining those records into one statement that “all law is current
through August 20” would overstate the evidence. The shorter judicial coverage is
not repaired by the longer legislative record.

## Use updating tools as leads to actual documents

A **[[citator]]** is a research tool that helps locate later history or treatment of
authorities. Its coverage and signals depend on the service and collection. A flag
can direct attention to a problem, but reading the later document is necessary to
understand its scope. The packet's small treatment record simulates that reasoning;
it is not a complete commercial citator or a claim that a live check occurred.

**[[Subsequent history]]** describes later proceedings in the same litigation, such
as a later appellate disposition. Later treatment can also come from a different
case citing the earlier case. Birch and Cedar are separately named disputes here;
B2's overruling is later treatment of Cedar, not a supplied later stage of Cedar's
own litigation. Keep these categories distinct so your note accurately describes
what happened rather than attaching a generic “appealed” label to every change.

**[[Negative treatment]]** is later authority that criticizes, limits, rejects or
otherwise undermines an earlier proposition in a legally relevant way. Those actions
do not all have the same effect. Read the later court's words, hierarchy and issue.
B2 expressly overrules Cedar's fifteen-day point. B3 expressly leaves Rowan's
message-form holding undisturbed. The presence of both case names in Birch does
not mean both suffered the same treatment.

## Update propositions, not just case names

**[[Proposition-specific analysis]]** asks how a later development affects the exact
claim for which you intend to use a source. A case may address several issues.
Do not turn a warning about one proposition into a claim that every sentence is
unusable, or turn a favorable reference to one proposition into a warranty about
every other issue. Cedar remains a historical document even though its deadline
proposition cannot control the later Larch analysis.

Statutory change needs the same precision. A1 changes the decision period for a
definitionally selected group of applications. It does not make Birch's account of
the old text historically false, and it does not change Rowan's analysis of savable
electronic form. Your entry can preserve the old holding while explaining the new
statutory context. “Overruled” and “amended” describe different mechanisms and should
not be used interchangeably.

A **[[coverage cutoff]]** is the date through which a source says its collection or
updates extend. A **[[research gap]]** is an unresolved portion of the investigation.
The August 16–20 judicial interval is a concrete gap, not a vague disclaimer. Specify
the source you would need next and how the uncertainty limits the conclusion. Avoid
claiming that no later case exists merely because no later case is supplied.

### Example 1: follow a warning to its scope

Start with Cedar C2, the fifteen-day proposition. IDX2 points to Birch B2. First
confirm that the later source is a published majority of Larch's highest court
under P2. Second read B2's reason: sections 2 and 4 do not permit the agency to
lengthen the period. Third record the express overruling of Cedar on that point.

Now inspect B3 instead of assuming every earlier case is rejected. B3 preserves
Rowan's electronic-message holding. Your authority entries therefore differ:
Cedar's fifteen-day proposition is displaced; Rowan's supplied form holding remains
usable within the packet, subject to the stated updating limits. This conclusion
comes from the later text, not from the color or existence of a treatment flag.

### Example 2: a truthful statement of incomplete currency

A researcher writes, “Checked today; all cases good through August 20.” Replace
that with a traceable statement: “Reviewed IDX2, covering the specified published
Larch courts through August 15. Read Birch B2–B3. Cedar's fifteen-day point is
overruled; Birch expressly leaves Rowan's form holding undisturbed. No check for
August 16–20, unpublished material or a full docket was possible under ACCESS1.”

Then state the next action: search an appropriately current court collection or
citator for later developments and inspect any relevant documents. This is a plan,
not a completed check. You can still answer the bounded exercise using the supplied
authorities, as long as you do not present the answer as a complete real-world
currency determination. Accuracy includes the limits of your work.

## Practice with feedback

Suppose the rule register lists no amendment to 8.3. Can you use its fifteen-day
text without further checking? Feedback: no. Absence of a textual amendment answers
one question; Birch B2's treatment and section 4's hierarchy answer another. The
compiled words can remain unchanged while their use is legally displaced.

Next, the legislative register is complete through August 20. Does that close the
case-index gap? Feedback: no. The registers cover different kinds of developments.
A complete amendment check cannot establish the absence of later judicial
interpretations. State each completed check with its own scope.

Finally, imagine an index shows a case was “distinguished.” What should you do?
Read the later decision to identify the issue, factual distinction, court and effect
on your proposition. Do not automatically equate distinction with overruling. The
packet supplies an express overruling for Cedar; real labels require comparable
attention to what the underlying source actually says.

## Common mistakes

A recent access date is not a coverage date. No recorded negative treatment is not
a guarantee of validity. A case name appearing in another opinion does not tell you
whether it was followed, limited, criticized or mentioned for background. Treating
all sources as having one shared cutoff hides gaps. Finally, do not report that a
paid tool or docket was checked when the exercise makes it unavailable.

## Key points

- Read the later source and record treatment of the exact proposition.
- Separate subsequent history, later treatment and statutory amendment.
- Record collection scope and coverage cutoff for each check.
- Explain unresolved gaps and the specific follow-up they require.

lessons.title: Check jurisdiction, hierarchy and source reliability
lessons.body:
## Four questions that should not collapse into one

A research result can be genuine, current and still wrong for your question. Ask
separately where it comes from, whether the copy is reliable, how current the
research is, and whether the proposition applies in the forum. A document's official
appearance cannot answer all four. This lesson uses the Larch and Maren materials
to practice keeping those questions distinct.

**[[Jurisdiction]]** here identifies the legal system whose authority is relevant; the
word can also concern a tribunal's power, which would require its own analysis in
a real matter. Our packet stipulates the Larch forum and supplies no federal issue.
Do not invent a jurisdictional dispute or import a real state's hierarchy. Use P2–P3
for this exercise, and research the actual rules separately when transferring the
method to a real assignment.

## Explain why an authority binds

**[[Binding authority]]** is authority the deciding forum must follow for the relevant
proposition under the applicable legal system. **[[Persuasive authority]]** may inform
reasoning without requiring that result. These labels are relational. They depend
on forum, source, proposition and status; they are not permanent badges attached
to every document from an institution.

A **[[hierarchy]]** orders institutions or sources for resolving conflicts under the
applicable rules. P2 gives Larch Supreme Court holdings priority over inconsistent
Court of Appeals holdings. P3 gives the statute priority over an inconsistent
agency regulation. The date of a source is relevant, but “newest document wins”
is not a general hierarchy rule. A recent staff memo does not amend a statute.
A recent Maren decision does not replace the Larch legislature's deadline.

**[[Applicability]]** asks whether the particular rule and version address these facts,
this issue and this forum. Even a binding institution's decision can concern a
different statutory text or leave the question open. Rowan helps with savable
messages, not an unspecified damages remedy. A1 chooses the period by receipt
date, so two pending applications can lawfully fall under different versions.

## Verify the document without overstating verification

**[[Authentication]]** concerns evidence that a document is what it purports to be and
comes from the identified source. **[[Integrity]]** concerns whether the content has
been changed from the verified version. GPO's authentication explanation describes
digital signatures for evidence of authenticity and integrity in its PDFs. Such
evidence does not establish that later legislation or decisions have left the legal
rule unchanged. An authentic old law can still need updating.

A visible seal or a downloaded file is not itself proof that you performed a
signature validation. Record the verification method actually used and any limits.
The fictional packet is authored teaching material; it contains no real judicial
certificates or digital signatures. Its stable labels support the exercise, but do
not claim official authenticity for Larch institutions that do not exist.

For outside research, prefer an identifiable issuing institution or reliable
publisher and keep document metadata. Compare suspicious discrepancies with an
authoritative copy and investigate version differences. Avoid casually merging two
versions because their titles match. A typographical correction, amended opinion
or different effective version can matter. If verification is incomplete, record
that fact instead of substituting confidence for evidence.

### Example 1: the highest court of the wrong jurisdiction

Elm is a published majority of Maren's Supreme Court, dated June 1, Year 5. A student
argues that it must control because it comes from a supreme court and is newer than
Birch. Start with P2: Maren is a different jurisdiction and its decisions do not bind
Larch trial courts. Next read E1–E2: the result follows a separate twenty-day statute.

Elm might be recorded as comparative background, but it does not supply the Larch
deadline. Neither its date nor its court's rank within Maren changes that mismatch.
A good authority entry explains the reason for exclusion: foreign jurisdiction and
different operative text. Merely marking it “bad source” would lose the distinction
between a valid document and an inapplicable proposition.

### Example 2: the newest agency document is not an amendment

M1 is a June 20 staff memo, later than Birch and later than A's enactment. It says
to use fourteen days for every application still pending July 1. First classify it:
nonbinding staff guidance under P3. Second compare its rule with A1, which selects
by receipt date and expressly preserves ten days for earlier receipts.

Third apply the conflict to Noor. Receipt June 25 places Noor in the older category,
even though the application remains pending in July. M1 does not override A1.
Record M1 as a rejected lead and explain the discrepancy. The reasoning depends on
source authority and text, not on speculation that staff acted dishonestly or on a
blanket claim that agency publications are never useful.

## Practice with feedback

Classify three propositions for a Larch trial court within the packet: Birch rejects
Cedar's fifteen-day rule; Elm permits twenty days under Maren's statute; G2 explains
Birch for students. Feedback: Birch's relevant published majority holding binds
under P2; Elm's foreign holding does not bind Larch and concerns different text;
G2 is secondary explanatory material whose leads require primary-source checking.
Each classification should include its reason, not just a one-word label.

Now suppose an authentic copy of the January guide is found on its publisher's site.
Does authenticity establish that fifteen days governs Ivo? Feedback: no. Provenance
and integrity concern the copy. Currency and applicability require Birch, A1 and
the receipt date. The guide remains a real copy of an outdated explanation within
the fictional scenario.

Finally, consider Rule 8.1 and Rule 8.3. Both come from the same regulation. Do they
necessarily have the same usable authority? Feedback: no. The packet provides
completeness requirements in 8.1, while 8.3 conflicts with section 4 and is rejected
in Birch. Evaluate each proposition rather than assigning one undifferentiated
status to every sentence in a document.

## Common mistakes

“Supreme Court” without a jurisdiction can conceal a forum mismatch. “Government
publication” without document type can conceal the difference between legislation
and guidance. “Digitally authenticated” without an update check can conceal obsolete
law. “Primary source” without hierarchy or applicability can conceal an unusable
proposition. These distinctions are tools for explaining a conclusion, not boxes
to tick without reading.

## Key points

- State the forum and the supplied hierarchy before ranking sources.
- Explain binding or persuasive status for the particular proposition.
- Keep authenticity and integrity separate from currency and applicability.
- Resolve source conflicts using their authority, text and relevant dates.

lessons.title: Cite precisely and preserve a source’s meaning
lessons.body:
## A citation is part of the reasoning

A **[[citation]]** identifies the source supporting a statement and directs the reader
to the relevant location. It is more than a formatting exercise. If a reader follows
your reference, the cited passage should support the proposition at the level of
generality you claimed. An elegant citation cannot repair an irrelevant source or
a misquoted sentence. This lesson practices traceability using the packet's stable
labels, then explains how to transfer the method to an assigned citation system.

For this course, use the teaching convention in the Citation and currency reference.
A full case reference can be “Birch, B2 (Larch Supreme Court, April 15, Year 5).”
For statutes, identify the section and version or amendment. These are exercise
locators, not fictional reporter volumes presented as genuine citations. In actual
coursework or litigation, follow the relevant assignment instructions, court rules
and citation guide rather than assuming this simplified format is sufficient.

## Give the reader source identity and a precise location

**[[Attribution]]** assigns words or ideas to the person or institution that expressed
them. H1 is an editorial summary, not Rowan's judicial holding. M1 is a staff memo,
not the legislature's transition provision. A citation to the correct document with
the wrong speaker attribution can still mislead. Before formatting, ask who said
it, in which document, and with what authority.

A useful source record preserves title or case name, issuer, date or applicable
version, and a pinpoint locator. A URL can help retrieval but should not be the
only identity information when a fuller citation is required. Links can change;
source identity and stable locators help another reader recover the document.
Your private research log can retain filenames, access dates and navigation steps
without forcing every working note into the final citation.

A **[[short form]]** is a shortened citation used after the source is clearly identified.
In this exercise, “Birch, B2” is adequate after an unambiguous full reference. “Id.”
or a bare page number can become confusing when paragraphs are rearranged or several
sources intervene. Do not use a shorthand you cannot verify in its current context.
The appropriate short-form rules for real work depend on the governing style.

## Quote words exactly and paraphrase ideas accurately

A **[[quotation]]** reproduces source language as such. A **[[paraphrase]]** restates a
source's idea in your own words. Both require accurate attribution and support.
Removing quotation marks does not free you to broaden the proposition, and changing
a few words does not eliminate the need to cite the source. Compare your sentence
against the original passage and its surrounding qualifications.

An **[[ellipsis]]** marks omitted material under the applicable style. A **[[bracketed alteration]]** visibly marks an insertion or change within quoted material when the
style permits it. These devices can improve readability, but they must not distort
meaning. Preserve limiting words, conditions and exceptions. If a short quote would
require confusing surgery, use an accurate paraphrase with a precise citation instead.

Check the actual source version, not a cached snippet or your earlier notes. Copying
from a summary can silently convert the editor's interpretation into judicial text.
Quotation review also includes speaker, context and scope: who is being quoted within
the opinion, whether the court adopts the proposition, and whether a later passage
limits it. Exact words can still be misleading when detached from those features.

### Example 1: fix an altered quotation

A draft states: “Section 3 allows an ‘electronic message,’ so even an unsavable chat
is sufficient.” The source actually permits a “savable electronic message.” First
restore the limiting word. Second check Rowan R3, which expressly leaves unsavable
messages unresolved. Third revise the conclusion rather than simply repairing the
quotation marks.

A supported version is: “Section 3 permits a ‘savable electronic message’; Rowan
accepted the specified savable message and reserved the unsavable-message question
(Act section 3; Rowan, R2–R3).” The revised statement separates statutory wording
from the case's application and limitation. It does not infer a rule about an
unresolved factual situation. Citation accuracy and substantive accuracy work together.

### Example 2: cite the transition rule that does the work

A note says, “Noor has ten days, Act section 2.” That identifies the old number,
but an August reader might reasonably ask why the fourteen-day amendment does not
apply. Add the source that resolves the issue: Amendment A, A1, which preserves
ten days for applications received before July 1.

A fuller explanation is: “Because Noor's complete application was received June 25,
A1 preserves the original section 2's ten-day period even though the deadline falls
in July.” Cite both provisions with the original version and amendment dates in
the initial references. The citation now shows the legal path from fact to rule.
By contrast, citing M1 would point to a conflicting nonbinding instruction rather
than the controlling transition text.

## Practice with feedback

Rewrite “H1 says all electronic messages count, therefore Rowan held that all
messages count.” Feedback: identify H1 as editorial, then state R2's narrower
savable-message result and R3's reservation. You may cite H1 when criticizing the
summary, but cite Rowan for the court's actual position. Do not silently assign
the editor's words to the judges.

Next, inspect this reference: “Source: page 2.” What is missing? Feedback: source
identity, version or date, issuer when needed, and a meaningful location system.
A viewer page alone does not distinguish the Act from an opinion or different
editions. In the packet, stable labels such as A1 and B2 are clearer.

Finally, paraphrase B2 without using a direct quotation. A sound version is: “Birch
rejected the agency's fifteen-day allowance because sections 2 and 4 did not authorize
it, and overruled Cedar on that point.” Cite B2. The paraphrase preserves the source's
scope and reason. It does not claim that Birch ruled on Amendment A, which did not
yet exist, or on remedies, which B3 reserves.

## Common mistakes

Do not fabricate missing reporter, docket or page information. Locate it or use an
appropriate available citation form. Do not assume every source requires the same
kind of date. A version date can matter more than an access date for selecting
historical law. Do not use an ellipsis to remove a condition that defeats your
argument. And do not treat proofreading punctuation as the end of citation review;
verify that each passage supports the sentence beside it.

## Key points

- Identify the source, applicable version and precise supporting passage.
- Attribute language to the correct speaker or institution.
- Preserve conditions and limitations in quotations and paraphrases.
- Apply the assigned citation rules; never invent missing citation data.

lessons.title: Build a reproducible research portfolio
lessons.body:
## Turn your work into something another reader can inspect

The final product of research is not a collection of open tabs. It is an explanation
of what supports the answer, how you found and checked it, and what remains unresolved.
A **[[research log]]** records the questions, collections, queries, results, passages
and next actions used during the investigation. An **[[authority table]]** organizes
the sources by the propositions they support, their status, versions and limitations.
These products complement each other: the log documents the process, while the table
makes the source analysis easy to compare.

On a phone, a table can be a sequence of labelled entries using the same fields.
The educational goal is not a wide grid. It is a complete record that another
researcher can follow. Use the Research workbench template and the Research portfolio
reference. All required research occurs within the supplied fictional packet; an
optional external orientation exercise is separate from the scored questions.

## Preserve an honest trail of completed work

An **[[audit trail]]** is the traceable record connecting inputs, actions and conclusions.
For research, it includes exact queries or navigation paths, active fields and
filters, collection scope, document versions and the passages examined. A list of
URLs is incomplete because it does not reveal which proposition was tested or what
the search excluded. Record unsuccessful searches as well as useful results.

Distinguish three statuses in your notes: performed and supported; performed but
unresolved; planned but not performed. This prevents a polished final document from
concealing uncertainty. An **[[access limitation]]** is a barrier to examining a needed
source or collection. ACCESS1 supplies several: no live database, paid citator or
full docket is available, and the packet cannot fill the August 16–20 judicial gap.
Do not claim those checks happened because they would be normal in another setting.

A **[[stopping rule]]** specifies when to pause research and report the bounded result.
It can depend on resolving the assigned issues, reviewing necessary sources, checking
contradictions and identifying remaining gaps. It is not “stop when the first source
agrees” or “keep searching until certainty is absolute.” Time and access constraints
can require a qualified conclusion. State the consequence of the missing work so
readers know how much weight to put on the result.

## Explain the result at the level your evidence supports

A **[[handoff]]** gives another researcher the findings, open questions and concrete next
steps needed to continue. “Research more” is too vague. “Check post-August-15 Larch
judicial developments for treatment of the deadline and form propositions, using
an appropriately current court collection or citator” identifies a source category,
period and issue. Do not pretend a negative search will necessarily prove that no
unseen authority exists; assess its coverage too.

**[[Self-assessment]]** uses stated criteria to identify strengths and revisions in your
own work. The portfolio rubric has six categories, each scored zero to two. It is
a learning aid, not faculty grading, credit or certification. The objective quizzes
can check a bounded answer, such as the receipt-date trigger. They cannot automatically
evaluate the completeness or persuasive quality of your whole research portfolio.

For the capstone, prepare at least seven primary-source entries plus evaluated guide
and memo leads, six log entries and a 450–650-word explanatory note. Answer both
Noor and Ivo. Include a faithful quotation, precise locators, rejected competing
rules and the coverage limits. Keep the source table and log outside the note's
word target so that concision does not force you to omit essential records.

### Example 1: a log entry that someone can reproduce

Weak entry: “Found that Cedar is wrong.” Replace it step by step. Identify the task:
check the fifteen-day proposition. Identify the collection: IDX1, specified published
Larch opinions through August 15. Record the query: Cedar in full text. Record the
supplied hits: Cedar and Birch. Record passages opened: C2 and B2.

Then state the finding: Birch expressly overrules the fifteen-day point under the
hierarchy in P2. Finally, state the unresolved follow-up for August 16–20 and other
material outside the index's scope. Label the whole entry a packet exercise. This
record supports reproduction without claiming a live database search or relying on
your memory of what the search screen once showed.

### Example 2: a conclusion with a specific limit

Within the supplied authorities, Noor's June 25 receipt uses ten days and produces
a July 5 deadline. The July 8 decision is late. Ivo's July 3 receipt uses fourteen
days and produces a July 17 deadline. The July 18 decision is also late. Cite the
original section 2, A1 and P4 or Rule 8.2 for the reasoning.

Now add what the conclusion does not resolve: later judicial developments after
August 15 were not checked, no remedy rule is supplied, and silence is not approval
under section 5. These qualifications are tied to concrete source boundaries. They
do not erase the supported exercise answer, and they do not claim that unknown
later authority definitely changes it. The conclusion distinguishes known support
from unfinished inquiry.

## Practice with feedback

Draft one authority entry for Rule 8. A strong entry separates its parts: 8.1 supplies
completeness requirements; 8.2 supplies day-zero counting; 8.3's fifteen-day allowance
conflicts with section 4 and is rejected by Birch B2. Record the unchanged regulatory
text and judicial treatment as different facts. A single “valid/invalid” label for
the entire rule loses this useful precision.

Next, write a one-sentence next action for the case-law gap. Feedback: name the dates,
relevant courts or collection, propositions and need to inspect any found authorities.
“Check the internet” is not reproducible. Do not report the proposed action as a
completed search in the next line of your log.

Finally, use the rubric on your note before consulting the model. If you selected
the correct deadlines but omitted the research gap, that is a substantive revision
need, not a cosmetic issue. If your citations are immaculate but M1 controls your
transition analysis, revisit hierarchy and A1. Each criterion tests a different
part of the research process.

## Common mistakes

Do not replace analysis with the number of sources collected. Do not omit adverse
leads because the final answer rejects them; explaining rejection makes the work
reviewable. Do not call every check “complete” when different collections have
different cutoffs. And do not treat a high self-score as approval by a university
or lawyer. The portfolio demonstrates practice in a bounded fictional setting.

## Key points

- Use a log for process and an authority table for source analysis.
- Separate completed, unresolved and planned work.
- Give a bounded answer with specific gaps and follow-up actions.
- Revise against the rubric; objective quizzes do not grade the portfolio.

questions.stem: Which issue statement best defines the assigned research for Noor?
choices: Was a savable electronic decision sufficient without considering when it was sent?
What remedy follows from the delay if timeliness and relief are treated as one issue?
Which deadline applies to a complete application using the decision date as the transition trigger?
Was the July 8 decision timely for a complete Larch application received June 25?
questions.explanation: The assigned question is whether the July 8 decision was timely for the June 25 complete receipt in Larch. Form alone, the wrong transition event and an assumed remedy do not define that issue.

questions.stem: Which date selects Noor’s statutory period under A1?
choices: July 1, when the new rule first took effect for eligible receipts
June 25, when the complete application was received
August 20, when the research snapshot is set
July 8, when the Office sent its decision
questions.explanation: A1 classifies applications by their complete-application receipt date. Its July 1 boundary matters, but the relevant event to compare against it is Noor’s June 25 receipt.

questions.stem: The packet’s judicial index ends August 15, but the assignment asks for research as of August 20. What belongs in the plan?
choices: A completed August 20 case-law check based on the assignment’s requested date
A completed August 20 case-law check based on the legislative register’s date
A completed packet check plus a separately identified August 16–20 follow-up
An instruction to omit the cutoff because it is close to the requested date
questions.explanation: The target date does not extend the index’s coverage. Identify the performed check and the unavailable judicial follow-up separately; legislative coverage concerns a different source type.

questions.stem: The application may omit the requested room, and completeness is not stipulated in this variant. What should the researcher do first?
choices: Identify the missing fact and consult Rule 8.1 before choosing the clock’s start
Start the clock at the first contact regardless of the missing information
Treat uncertainty about completeness as proof that no deadline applies
Assume completeness because the Office eventually issued a decision
questions.explanation: Rule 8.1 specifies the completeness items. Uncertainty calls for a fact inquiry; it supports neither presumed completeness nor a final conclusion that the deadline never applies.

questions.stem: Why does the research plan name a Larch trial court as the forum?
choices: P2 ties the binding force of judicial holdings to that forum
P2 makes a case binding based on its caption rather than its relevant holding
P2 gives agency guidance the same force as the forum’s judicial holdings
P2 makes the most recent decision binding without comparing its jurisdiction
questions.explanation: P2 states which courts bind the Larch trial court. Naming the forum does not erase hierarchy, source distinctions or temporal applicability.

questions.stem: Which planning choice best manages a limited research budget?
choices: Prioritize convenient guide summaries, then defer checking their primary citations
Prioritize collecting more sources, then reconstruct their versions and coverage at the end
Prioritize the governing text, transition and adverse leads, then record unresolved work
Prioritize sources supporting the proposed answer, then treat agreement as a stopping point
questions.explanation: A budget should prioritize questions that can change the answer and preserve an honest handoff. It does not justify selective searching or concealing missing checks.

questions.stem: A researcher concludes that a late decision automatically awards a room. Which planning omission caused the overreach?
choices: Failing to distinguish the date the amendment was enacted from its effective date
Failing to distinguish a savable electronic decision from an unsavable electronic message
Failing to distinguish the date of receipt from the date the written decision was sent
Failing to separate the timeliness issue from the unsupplied remedy question
questions.explanation: The error is moving from lateness to entitlement without a remedy rule. Section 5 rejects approval by silence. Receipt, form and enactment/effectiveness distinctions matter elsewhere, but do not supply the missing remedy.

questions.stem: Which note accurately labels a planned search that ACCESS1 prevents?
choices: Complete: access limits make the later judicial interval immaterial
Not performed: search later judicial developments for August 16–20
Performed: the legislative register also cleared the later judicial interval
Performed: no later judicial developments exist for August 16–20
questions.explanation: An unperformed search must stay a planned action. Neither a legislative register nor lack of access proves the absence or irrelevance of later judicial developments.

questions.stem: Match each item in the research plan to its distinct role.
choices: Receipt-date trigger
Deciding forum
Research target date
Required output
questions.explanation: The event date selects the applicable period, the forum frames authority, the snapshot sets the desired research date, and the table/log/note specify the product.

questions.stem: A provisional statement filling a missing factual gap, which must be labelled and tested, is an ___.
questions.explanation: An assumption is provisional, not a supplied fact. Identify it and investigate it when it can change the result.

questions.stem: What is the best use of G2, the May guide, in an August inquiry?
choices: Confirm its quotations of Birch and treat that confirmation as an August update
Compare its edition with G1 and choose its conclusions without opening the cited text
Follow its case citations but treat its statutory account as settled for July receipts
Follow its primary-source leads and check developments after the guide’s date
questions.explanation: G2 is a useful secondary lead that incorporates Birch but predates A1. Its sources and later changes still require checking; relative newness is not final currency.

questions.stem: Which classification correctly describes Cedar after Birch overrules its fifteen-day point?
choices: A binding current deadline rule because primary sources cannot be displaced
A regulation because it discussed the Office’s fifteen-day rule
A primary judicial source whose deadline proposition has been displaced
A secondary source because a later court rejected its deadline proposition
questions.explanation: Primary/secondary classification describes the source’s nature. Later treatment changes the use of its proposition without turning an opinion into commentary or regulation.

questions.stem: IDX1 gives zero hits for “study room” in case titles. Which next step best addresses the likely search problem?
choices: Search “complete application” in full text and examine the supplied hits
Repeat the same title query and report it as a complete treatment check
Conclude that no Larch opinion concerns room applications
Use the zero result to disregard the cases named in the packet
questions.explanation: The captions use Town Room Office. A full-text query using the operative phrase returns Rowan, Cedar and Birch; zero title hits do not prove an absence of law.

questions.stem: Which information is essential to make a search query reproducible?
choices: The query and result count, with the service’s default fields and filters left unspecified
The topic and conclusions, with the actual query and searched collection left unspecified
The final sources and access date, with unsuccessful queries and coverage left unspecified
The query, searched field, active filters and collection coverage
questions.explanation: Reproduction requires the actual query, field, active filters and collection coverage. A result count, access date or conclusion without those settings can hide a different search scope.

questions.stem: G1 cites Cedar for fifteen days. What should a researcher do after confirming C2?
choices: Record C2’s wording as verified and treat verification as sufficient to use fifteen days
Use G1’s publication date as the end date of the necessary later-case inquiry
Look for later treatment and read Birch’s relevant passages
Check only for amendments to Rule 8.3 before deciding whether Cedar still supports fifteen days
questions.explanation: Confirmation establishes what Cedar said, not its later status. IDX2 leads to B2’s overruling; preserve the history while updating the proposition.

questions.stem: Why does G2’s May publication date matter for Ivo’s July application?
choices: It precedes Amendment A and prompts a later-legislation check
It supplies the relevant event date for selecting the statutory version for Ivo
It establishes that the ten-day rule remains applicable to every pending July application
It establishes Birch’s treatment and therefore also completes the later-legislation check
questions.explanation: G2 predates the amendment enacted June 10 and effective July 1. A1 and Ivo’s July 3 receipt, not the guide’s publication date alone, select the applicable period.

questions.stem: A guide cites an inaccessible case. Which entry is accurate?
choices: Verified absence: inaccessible cases cannot affect the assigned issue
Unverified lead: obtain the full case before attributing its holding
Completed search: infer the case’s reasoning from its title and date
Verified holding: the guide’s description substitutes for the unavailable case
questions.explanation: A missing full source remains an unverified lead. Record the access problem and next action rather than inventing reasoning or treating inaccessibility as irrelevance.

questions.stem: How should a researcher transfer a query between two search services?
choices: Keep the same words but omit filters from the research record
Check each service’s syntax and fields before assuming the same behavior
Treat matching result counts as proof that the collections are identical
Assume quotation marks and proximity connectors always work identically
questions.explanation: Syntax, fields, filters and coverage can differ. Consult the service’s instructions and document the actual query; equal counts do not establish equal content.

questions.stem: Match each packet source to its stated source category.
choices: Legislation
Commentary
Judicial opinion
Staff guidance
questions.explanation: The Act is legislation, Cedar is an opinion, G1 is commentary and M1 is nonbinding staff guidance. Category does not by itself settle currency or applicability.

questions.stem: A guide’s citation that points toward a source still needing examination is a research ___.
questions.explanation: A lead is a direction for further inquiry, not a verified holding or completed currency check.

questions.stem: A was enacted June 10 and became effective July 1. A complete application arrived June 20. Which period does A1 select?
choices: Twenty days, because Elm was already decided
Ten days, because receipt preceded July 1
Fourteen days, because receipt followed enactment
Fifteen days, because Rule 8.3 remains printed
questions.explanation: A1 uses receipt on or after its July 1 boundary, not the June 10 enactment date. This earlier receipt retains ten days under the original section 2.

questions.stem: Noor’s complete application arrived June 25. What is the deadline under P4 and A1?
choices: July 10, applying Rule 8.3’s fifteen-day period
July 5, using ten days with receipt as day zero
July 9, applying fourteen days because the deadline is in July
July 4, including the receipt day as day one
questions.explanation: A1 preserves ten days for June 25 receipt. June 26–30 are days one to five; July 1–5 are days six to ten. Receipt is day zero, and 8.3 cannot extend the statute.

questions.stem: Which source directly resolves whether an application pending July 1 keeps the old period?
choices: M1’s staff direction keyed to whether an application is still pending
G2’s May explanation without checking later legislation
A1’s transition provision keyed to complete-application receipt
Elm’s discussion of Maren’s twenty-day text
questions.explanation: A1 expressly preserves ten days for receipts before July 1. M1 conflicts with that criterion; G2 predates A and Elm concerns another jurisdiction.

questions.stem: What remains unchanged under A2?
choices: Sections 1, 2, 4 and 5 remain unchanged for all complete applications
Sections 1, 3 and 5 remain unchanged, but section 4 now permits fifteen-day rules
Sections 1, 3 and 4 remain unchanged, but section 5 now makes silence approval
Sections 1, 3, 4 and 5 of the Act
questions.explanation: A2 expressly leaves sections 1, 3, 4 and 5 unchanged. Section 2 changes for eligible receipts. There is no new fifteen-day exception in section 4 or approval-by-silence rule in section 5.

questions.stem: Why does section 4 matter when evaluating Rule 8.3?
choices: It limits the agency’s delegated power and forbids lengthening the period
It authorizes the agency to select the decision period when prescribing application forms
It permits the agency to extend the period for applications with all required information
It leaves a timing exception for an agency rule issued after the original statute’s enactment
questions.explanation: Section 4 delegates forms and identifying information but expressly forbids a longer decision period. Specificity, staff authorship and completeness do not create an exception.

questions.stem: Ivo’s complete application arrived July 3 and a paper decision was sent July 18. Which analysis follows the packet?
choices: Rule 8.3 allows fifteen days, ending July 18; the decision is timely
Paper form eliminates the need to apply a decision deadline
The original Act always allows ten days, ending July 13; A1 is irrelevant
A1 allows fourteen days, ending July 17; the decision is late
questions.explanation: Receipt on July 3 triggers A1. July 4 is day one and July 17 day fourteen. Section 4 and Birch reject using 8.3 to lengthen the period; paper form is a separate issue.

questions.stem: The rule register reports no textual amendment to 8.3. What follows?
choices: Birch has no effect until the agency physically deletes the rule’s text
Its fifteen-day allowance must govern because the compiler retained the words
Its wording is unchanged, but its usable authority still requires judicial and statutory checks
The absence of an amendment establishes the absence of later case law
questions.explanation: Textual currency is one check. The statute’s delegation limit and Birch’s treatment can defeat the fifteen-day proposition even while the regulation remains reproduced.

questions.stem: What does this packet establish about a remedy for a late decision?
choices: No remedy rule is supplied, and silence does not approve an application
A late decision establishes a damages right, while the amount remains outside the packet
A late decision establishes a right to the room, while only damages require further research
A late decision establishes an appeal right, while the filing deadline remains outside the packet
questions.explanation: Section 5 expressly rejects approval by silence and supplies no rule for remedies or appeal deadlines. A timeliness conclusion cannot fill those omissions.

questions.stem: Match each date to its role in selecting and calculating Noor’s deadline.
choices: Enactment date
Effective boundary
Receipt date
Decision deadline
questions.explanation: Enactment, effectiveness, event and deadline are separate. A1 selects the period by receipt, and P4 then calculates the deadline.

questions.stem: Under P4 and Rule 8.2, the receipt date is day ___.
questions.explanation: The following day is day one. Counting receipt as day one would shorten the supplied statutory period by a day.

questions.stem: What proposition does Rowan R2 support?
choices: A delivered electronic decision satisfies section 3 without checking whether it is savable
A savable electronic decision satisfies section 3 even if the required delivery never occurred
The specified savable electronic decision satisfies the packet’s writing requirement
A savable electronic decision satisfies the deadline whenever it meets section 3’s form rule
questions.explanation: R2 applies section 3 to the savable message described in R1. R3 reserves unsavable messages and remedies; form compliance does not eliminate the deadline.

questions.stem: Why is H1 insufficient to establish Rowan’s holding?
choices: Its placement with the opinion makes it judicial language unless the court expressly disclaims it
It is an editorial summary whose breadth must be checked against R2–R3
Its wording may be attributed to the court once the case name and decision date are verified
Its description of the outcome can substitute for checking the qualifications in R2–R3
questions.explanation: H1 is not judicial language and overstates the supplied result. Read and attribute R2–R3 rather than transferring the editor’s words to the court.

questions.stem: Which passage directly records Birch’s treatment of Rowan’s form holding?
choices: G1, which summarizes Cedar before Birch existed
E1, which applies a separate twenty-day statute
B3, which expressly leaves that holding undisturbed
C2, which endorses a fifteen-day decision period
questions.explanation: B3 expressly addresses Rowan. C2 and E1 concern different propositions, and G1 predates Birch; none substitutes for the later court’s statement.

questions.stem: What does Birch’s disposition establish in this packet?
choices: The timeliness ruling is affirmed on the view that Rule 8.3 permits the delay
The timeliness ruling is reversed and the room is awarded, while damages remain open
The timeliness ruling is reversed and damages are established, with only their amount remanded
The timeliness ruling is reversed and remanded without a decided remedy
questions.explanation: B3 reverses the timeliness ruling, remands and reserves remedies. It also preserves Rowan’s form holding. Reversal must be read with the specific ruling and relief addressed.

questions.stem: Which is a useful pinpoint locator for the overruling of Cedar’s fifteen-day point?
choices: Cedar, C2
Birch, B4
Birch, B1
Birch, B2
questions.explanation: B2 expressly overrules Cedar’s fifteen-day proposition. B1 describes the dispute; C2 states Cedar’s original rule; B4 confines Birch to the old text and directs attention to later legislation.

questions.stem: Which entry preserves both Cedar’s original proposition and its later treatment?
choices: C2 originally required ten days because B2 now says so
C2 adopted fifteen days; B2 later overruled that point
C2 remains controlling because a later decision cannot change its printed words
C2 became secondary commentary when Birch rejected its reasoning
questions.explanation: Record historical content and later legal effect separately. Overruling does not rewrite Cedar’s text or change an opinion’s classification into commentary.

questions.stem: Why should a researcher record opinion type and procedural posture?
choices: They help identify the authoritative voice and the issue the court actually resolved
They establish the case’s outcome and therefore identify the remedy without reading the disposition
They establish publication and court level and therefore make every passage equally binding
They establish the source’s procedural identity and therefore complete the later-treatment check
questions.explanation: Type and posture orient the reader to the speaker, task and result. They do not make every sentence binding, replace updating or determine relief from the caption.

questions.stem: A claim concerns an unsavable message. How should Rowan R3 affect the analysis?
choices: Record that Rowan reserved that question rather than claiming it decided the result
Omit R3 because it qualifies the broader language of the editorial summary
Treat the reservation as an affirmative holding that unsavable messages qualify
Treat the reservation as an affirmative holding that unsavable messages fail
questions.explanation: R3 expressly leaves the question unresolved. A reservation is neither approval nor rejection; report the boundary rather than inventing a holding.

questions.stem: Match each passage label to the kind of support or limitation it supplies.
choices: Savable-message holding
Reserved questions
Overruling of Cedar
Editorial summary
questions.explanation: R2 states the application to a savable message, R3 limits the decision, B2 supplies later treatment of Cedar, and H1 is editorial rather than judicial language.

questions.stem: The statement of what ruling a court is reviewing and how the case reached it is its procedural ___.
questions.explanation: Procedural posture identifies the court’s task and the ruling under review; it helps keep reversal separate from a final merits remedy.

questions.stem: What is the most accurate description of Birch’s relationship to Cedar?
choices: A later, separate case overruling Cedar’s fifteen-day proposition
A supplied later appellate stage within Cedar’s own litigation
A guide revision that changes Cedar from primary to secondary material
An amendment enacted by the legislature to replace Cedar’s text
questions.explanation: B2 supplies later treatment in a separately named dispute. The packet does not present Birch as subsequent proceedings in Cedar itself, legislation or commentary.

questions.stem: IDX2 flags Cedar’s fifteen-day proposition. What must the researcher do next?
choices: Apply the warning to every source Birch cites without comparing the individual passages
Record the warning against Cedar without checking whether the relevant proposition is affected
Treat the index’s warning as resolving both the original rule and the later amendment
Read Birch B2 and assess its court, reasoning and stated scope
questions.explanation: An updating signal leads to the actual later source. B2 identifies the proposition, reason and express overruling; the index’s August 15 cutoff still limits the check.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the supplied case-index coverage accurately?
choices: Specified published Larch opinions through August 15, with August 16–20 unchecked
All published and unpublished proceedings through August 15 including a full docket
All judicial developments through August 20 because AR1 reaches that date
