Every Larch legal source through August 20 because that is the research date
questions.explanation: IDX1 specifies the courts, publication scope and August 15 cutoff. ACCESS1 denies a full-docket and later-interval check; legislative coverage cannot extend it.

questions.stem: Why does no recorded amendment to Rule 8.3 fail to settle its usability?
choices: Only a formal regulatory amendment can change which period the unchanged text authorizes
Judicial treatment and the statutory delegation can defeat the unchanged proposition
The rule register’s current date makes a separate judicial-treatment check unnecessary
The absence of a textual amendment restores the period after a later statute changes section 2
questions.explanation: B2 rejects the fifteen-day proposition and section 4 forbids extending the statutory period. Textual amendment and judicial treatment are distinct checks; mere mention does not automatically invalidate a rule.

questions.stem: How does A1 affect the research use of Birch’s discussion of ten days?
choices: Assume A1 also rejects Rowan’s separate electronic-form holding
Treat Birch’s historical explanation as false because legislation later changed
Preserve Birch’s old-text analysis while applying A1’s new period to eligible receipts
Rewrite Birch as if it had decided the later fourteen-day amendment
questions.explanation: B4 confines Birch to the original text. A1 changes the period for defined receipts and A2 leaves section 3 unchanged; the later amendment neither rewrites history nor decides electronic-form issues.

questions.stem: Which update note is supported by IDX2?
choices: B2 replaces Cedar’s timing point and also rejects Rowan’s earlier electronic-form holding
B3 preserves Rowan and thereby preserves Cedar’s separate fifteen-day proposition as well
B2 criticizes Cedar’s timing point but leaves it binding because the regulation is still printed
B2 overrules Cedar’s timing point; B3 leaves Rowan’s form holding undisturbed
questions.explanation: Treatment must be read proposition by proposition. The two passages explicitly assign different effects; citation, index inclusion and case-name presence alone do not show the treatment.

questions.stem: A service labels a later case as distinguishing an earlier case. What should a researcher infer before reading it?
choices: The earlier case has necessarily been overruled for every proposition
There is a lead requiring examination of the issue and factual distinction
The later case can be ignored because distinction never matters
The earlier case is necessarily binding on the new facts without analysis
questions.explanation: A label signals an inquiry. Read the later reasoning, facts, court and proposition before deciding whether the distinction affects your use of the earlier case.

questions.stem: Which is the best handoff for the August 16–20 gap?
choices: Write “no cases found” without performing a search of that interval
State that lack of access proves later cases would not change the conclusion
Identify the unsearched interval and relevant propositions for a current court or citator check
Extend IDX2’s coverage to the assignment date in the final table
questions.explanation: The handoff should name the gap and a specific next source/action. An unperformed check supports no negative finding or invented extension of coverage.

questions.stem: Match each updating record to its actual coverage or limit.
choices: Statute changes: Aug 20
Rule edits: Aug 20
Case treatment: Aug 15
Unavailable checks
questions.explanation: The records cover different materials and dates. AR1 and the rule note cannot fill IDX2’s judicial gap; ACCESS1 identifies unperformed work.

questions.stem: The date through which an index says its updates extend is its coverage ___.
questions.explanation: The cutoff describes the source’s update boundary. It is not automatically the date on which you accessed or used the index.

questions.stem: Why does Elm’s June decision not supply the Larch deadline?
choices: It applies Maren’s different statute and does not bind the Larch forum under P2
Its later date makes its twenty-day rule controlling unless Larch expressly rejects Elm by name
Its supreme-court status controls the deadline despite the different statutory wording
Its foreign origin changes the decision into secondary commentary rather than judicial material
questions.explanation: P2 makes Maren foreign to the Larch forum, and E1–E2 apply different twenty-day text. Elm remains a primary judicial source; neither its later date nor its court’s rank within Maren makes it binding in Larch.

questions.stem: Why does M1 fail to control Noor’s pending application?
choices: Its later date makes it an application of A1 that the court must follow without comparing the text
Its pending-status criterion matches A1 because the relevant event is the July decision date
Nonbinding staff guidance conflicts with A1’s receipt-date transition
Its guidance is invalid solely because staff issued it, regardless of its consistency with A1
questions.explanation: P3 classifies M1 as nonbinding and A1 expressly preserves ten days for pre-July receipts. M1 instead uses pending status; its more recent issuance does not amend the statute.

questions.stem: An old statute is obtained as a verified, unaltered copy from its issuer. What does that check establish by itself?
choices: That the same statutory version governs every earlier and later event
That its legal coverage necessarily extends through the date of download
That no amendment has been enacted since that version was issued
The verified copy’s identity and integrity, with later legal developments still needing review
questions.explanation: Verifying the copy addresses identity and alteration. It does not prove the absence of amendments, establish applicability to every event or extend the source’s currency to the access date.

questions.stem: What does “primary source” establish about a case by itself?
choices: Its formal issuance by a court, which alone settles binding force in the present forum
Its nature as judicial material, not automatic binding force for the present proposition
Its historical content, which alone establishes that later courts have left it unchanged
Its document type, which alone verifies the accuracy of every copy and quoted excerpt
questions.explanation: Primary classification does not decide hierarchy, forum relationship, current status or the reliability of a particular copy. Cedar and Elm illustrate different additional inquiries.

questions.stem: Which assessment of Rule 8 is most precise?
choices: Use 8.1 for completeness, 8.2 for counting, and separately address 8.3’s conflict
Accept all subsections because they appear in a single regulation
Reject every subsection merely because Birch rejects the fifteen-day point
Treat its staff origin as permission to override every statutory condition
questions.explanation: The packet supplies 8.1 and 8.2 for distinct tasks. B2 and section 4 reject the longer-period proposition; that does not erase every other part of the regulation.

questions.stem: A verified old copy of G1 is obtained. What additional inquiry matters for Ivo’s deadline?
choices: Use the guide’s cited case after confirming its original wording, without checking later treatment
Check the guide’s issuer and copy integrity again, treating that as sufficient for current use
Check later primary developments and whether their versions apply to July 3 receipt
Compare the guide’s publication date with receipt, without reading later primary developments
questions.explanation: Source verification concerns the copy. Birch, A1 and the event date determine later legal use; a genuine old guide can still contain an outdated explanation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the Larch packet’s authority?
choices: Its stable paragraph labels establish legal validity outside the course
It supplies fictional rules for a bounded exercise, not authentic real court documents
Its official-looking labels certify that real Larch courts issued the opinions
Its original authorship substitutes for a real-world signature or docket check
questions.explanation: The reference explicitly labels every institution and document fictional. Stable teaching labels enable retrieval and practice, not real-world authentication or legal authority.

questions.stem: What should an authority-table entry explain when labelling Birch binding?
choices: Its highest-court title and publication date without identifying the jurisdiction and relevant issue
Its agreement with the intended result without identifying the rule that gives it binding force
Its primary-source classification without identifying which holding applies in the stated forum
Its relevant published majority holding and the Larch hierarchy supplied by P2
questions.explanation: Binding force is relational: identify forum, deciding institution, opinion type and relevant holding under P2. An institution label without jurisdiction, date alone or agreement with a desired result is insufficient.

questions.stem: Match each verification question to the distinct concept it tests.
left: Source is what it purports to be
Rule fits this forum, event and issue
choices: Integrity
Authentication
Currency
Applicability
questions.explanation: Integrity concerns alteration, authentication concerns source identity, currency concerns later developments, and applicability concerns fit. Passing one does not prove the others.

questions.stem: Authority that may inform a court’s reasoning without requiring its result is ___ authority.
questions.explanation: Persuasive authority may be considered without binding the forum. Its weight still depends on the proposition, reasoning and context.

questions.stem: Which quotation-based statement preserves section 3’s meaning?
choices: It permits an “electronic message,” so savability is legally irrelevant
It permits a “savable electronic message,” so every such message is automatically timely
It permits a “savable electronic message,” subject to the stated application and limits
It permits a “savable electronic message,” so a late decision necessarily earns damages
questions.explanation: Preserve the limiting word and separate form from timing and remedies. Exact quoted words do not support additional propositions the source never states.

questions.stem: A note explains why Noor keeps ten days despite a July deadline. Which citations best support that reasoning?
choices: Elm E1 and its twenty-day Maren statute
Original Act section 2 and Amendment A, A1
M1’s pending-application direction and G1’s Cedar summary
Rowan R3 alone, which reserves unsavable messages and remedies
questions.explanation: Section 2 supplies ten days and A1 preserves that period for pre-July receipts. The other sources conflict, address another jurisdiction, or do not resolve the transition.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly attributes H1?
choices: The editor’s wording can be attributed to the court once its described outcome matches the disposition
The court adopted the summary’s words because it appears with the opinion’s identifying heading
The summary is part of R2’s holding because it discusses the same electronic-message issue
An editor broadly summarized Rowan; the opinion’s narrower text must be checked
questions.explanation: H1 is expressly editorial and broader than R2–R3. Placement beside a primary source does not make it judicial, legislative or regulatory language.

questions.stem: When is “Birch, B2” an acceptable short reference under this course’s convention?
choices: After Birch has been clearly identified and the reference is unambiguous
After placing Birch in a source list, even if the text uses an ambiguous shortened reference
After identifying Birch, even if B2 is replaced with an unexplained viewer page number
After any earlier mention of a Larch case, even if Birch has not been identified
questions.explanation: A short form must point unambiguously to a source already identified and retain a useful locator. Mentioning another Larch case, using an unexplained viewer page or relying on an ambiguous source-list reference does not suffice.

questions.stem: What should a researcher do when the source lacks an expected reporter volume?
choices: Find the information or use an appropriate available citation form without inventing it
Use another case’s reporter information if the parties have similar names
Delete the source identity and retain only a generic “online opinion” label
Invent a plausible volume so the citation resembles familiar examples
questions.explanation: Missing citation data requires retrieval or an appropriate supported form. Fabricated or borrowed details obstruct verification, and a generic label loses source identity.

questions.stem: Which paraphrase accurately represents Birch B2?
choices: Birch decides that all late applicants receive their requested rooms
Birch rejects the unauthorized fifteen-day rule and overrules Cedar on that point
Birch interprets Amendment A to give every pending application fourteen days
Birch rejects all agency rules, including completeness and day-zero counting
questions.explanation: B2 addresses the original deadline and section 4’s limit. A had not yet been enacted, and the packet does not support eliminating all regulations or awarding a remedy.

questions.stem: What is wrong with removing “savable” from a quotation to make the rule cover unsavable chats?
choices: The change is acceptable whenever the writer prefers the broader interpretation
Every shortened quotation is forbidden even when its meaning remains intact
Only the absence of a URL matters; the omitted condition has no effect
The omission changes a material condition instead of preserving the source’s meaning
questions.explanation: An omission must not distort meaning. Here savability is expressly required and R3 reserves the unsavable-message question. Not all shortening is impermissible, but this one alters the rule.

questions.stem: Why does a paraphrase of a source still need a citation?
choices: It requires a citation only if it retains the source’s distinctive wording rather than the underlying idea
It requires a citation only if the paraphrase expresses uncertainty about the source’s meaning
It attributes the underlying idea and lets the reader check its support
It can cite a search summary as the opinion’s reasoning without inspecting the source passage
questions.explanation: Paraphrases must represent and attribute the source accurately. Changing wording does not eliminate the need to verify and cite the supporting passage.

questions.stem: Match each writing device to its function, keeping accuracy and attribution requirements in mind.
choices: Exact source words
Idea in new wording
Omission marker
Visible quoted edit
questions.explanation: Quotations and paraphrases both need support. Ellipses and brackets disclose permitted changes; they do not authorize distortion of the original meaning.

questions.stem: A reference that identifies the exact supporting paragraph, page or section is a ___ locator.
questions.explanation: A pinpoint directs the reader to the supporting passage. In this course B2 and A1 are stable teaching locators, not invented reporter page numbers.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a research log and an authority table?
choices: The log records the investigation; the table organizes sources, propositions and status
The log organizes source holdings; the table records queries and search-filter changes
The log records access dates; the table treats those dates as proof that updating is complete
The log records only successful searches; the table records the rest without their coverage
questions.explanation: The log records the search process, including unsuccessful searches and scope. The authority table organizes sources, propositions and status. Reversing those roles or treating access dates as completed updates defeats their purposes.

questions.stem: Which log entry is reproducible for the Cedar update exercise?
choices: IDX1; Cedar in full text; hits Cedar/Birch; result recorded as current through August 20 without a later check
G1 cited Cedar; C2 confirmed; later treatment recorded as checked without opening Birch or IDX2
IDX1 through August 15; Cedar/Birch; no field, passage or follow-up recorded for the treatment conclusion
IDX1 through August 15; Cedar in full text; hits Cedar/Birch; read C2/B2; later interval unsearched
questions.explanation: Only the complete entry identifies IDX1’s cutoff, full-text query, hits, examined passages and open interval. The alternatives extend coverage, omit reproducible steps or claim a later check that was not done.

questions.stem: What conclusion follows for both capstone files within the supplied authorities?
choices: Both decisions are timely because 8.3 permits fifteen days for every application
Both applicants automatically receive rooms because the decisions were late
Both decisions are late; neither automatic approval nor a remedy follows from the packet
Noor’s July deadline switches that application to fourteen days; Noor is timely and Ivo is late
questions.explanation: Noor’s deadline is July 5 and Ivo’s July 17; their decisions follow those dates. A1 preserves Noor’s old period, 8.3 cannot extend the statute, and section 5 prevents approval by silence.

questions.stem: Which stopping rule best fits the portfolio assignment?
choices: Resolve the main calculation and omit the remaining coverage gaps because they cannot be closed
Resolve every imaginable issue before reporting, even where the assignment supplies no applicable rule
Resolve the supplied issues and contradictions, document gaps, and specify the remaining checks
Resolve the issue using the first primary source and stop before checking competing authority
questions.explanation: The assignment calls for a supported, bounded answer and honest handoff. Source count, confirmation alone and impossible absolute certainty are not suitable completion criteria.

questions.stem: What should the authority entry for Rule 8 explain?
choices: The rule’s current wording and effective date, omitting judicial treatment from its authority entry
Different uses of 8.1 and 8.2, plus the conflict and treatment affecting 8.3
The adverse treatment of 8.3, treating that as rejection of the entire regulation including 8.1–8.2
The common publisher and unchanged text, treating all subsections as equally usable for the deadline
questions.explanation: The subsections answer different questions. Record completeness and counting separately from the invalid longer-period proposition, with section 4 and B2 explaining the conflict.

questions.stem: The portfolio has accurate deadlines but claims a live paid-citator check that never occurred. What revision is required?
choices: Remove the false completion claim and state the actual packet check and access limits
Retain the completion label but add a general access disclaimer without identifying the unperformed check
Replace the citator name with “later treatment reviewed” while still including August 16–20 as checked
Record the index review as a full-docket check because both would investigate judicial developments
questions.explanation: Correct results do not justify false process claims. The log must describe performed work and identify unavailable checks without disguising them.

questions.stem: What does a high portfolio self-assessment score establish?
choices: A completed substantive assessment of the portfolio by the app’s objective-question grader
A finding that the research meets external law-school standards without further review
A completed currency check for the underlying sources through the learner’s scoring date
A learner’s rubric-based review to guide revision, not faculty grading or credit
questions.explanation: The rubric is the learner’s review to guide revision. It is not the app’s automatic grading of the portfolio, external school assessment or a completed update of the underlying sources.

questions.stem: Which final note most accurately states the currency limitation?
choices: The judicial gap can be omitted because the requested note has a word target
Legislative/rule registers reach August 20; the case index stops August 15, leaving later judicial checks open
No later cases exist because none appears after the case index’s cutoff
All law is current through August 20 because one register reaches that date
questions.explanation: State source-specific coverage. A note’s word target does not justify concealing an unresolved judicial interval; neither a legislative register nor index silence proves it closed.

questions.stem: Match each portfolio component to its distinct function.
choices: Search-process record
Source analysis
Open research gap
Learner self-review
questions.explanation: Process, source analysis, limitations and self-review play different roles. Together they support a reproducible, bounded conclusion without claiming outside approval.

questions.stem: The product that records queries, collections, results and next actions as research proceeds is a research ___.
questions.explanation: A research log records the investigation. An authority table complements it by organizing the sources and their support, status and limits.

cards.front: What belongs in a research plan?
cards.back: A written account of the issue, forum, facts, scope, sources and next actions that will guide an investigation.

cards.front: How does an issue statement improve on “research room law”?
cards.back: It replaces a broad topic with a question tied to the forum, event dates and disputed rule. For Noor, ask whether the July 8 decision was timely for a complete application received June 25.

cards.front: Why identify the forum before ranking cases?
cards.back: The tribunal or setting in which the legal issue would be decided; it affects which authority binds.

cards.front: Why record receipt date separately from research date?
cards.back: Receipt selects the applicable statutory period under A1. The research date sets the intended update horizon. One date cannot substitute for the other.

cards.front: How should a missing fact be handled provisionally?
cards.back: A provisional statement used to fill a missing fact, which should be labelled and tested if it can affect the answer.

cards.front: What does research scope make explicit?
cards.back: The issues, jurisdictions, periods and collections included in an investigation, together with its stated boundaries.

cards.front: How does the deliverable affect what you record while researching?
cards.back: The requested product determines what evidence you must preserve. A log needs queries and coverage; an authority table needs propositions, versions and treatment; a note needs traceable support and limits.

cards.front: Noor: what dates and forum belong in the plan?
cards.back: Larch trial court; receipt June 25, decision July 8 and research snapshot August 20, Year 5. The case index covers only through August 15.

cards.front: What can a secondary source contribute before primary-source checking?
cards.back: It can introduce terminology, organize issues and point to primary sources. Follow and update those leads instead of treating the explanation as binding law.

cards.front: Why can an overruled case still be a primary source?
cards.back: It remains the court’s historical opinion. Overruling changes the use of the affected proposition, not the document’s primary-source classification; Cedar C2 and Birch B2 illustrate this.

cards.front: What should you record to establish source provenance?
cards.back: Information about where a document came from, who issued it and which version or publication is being examined.

cards.front: Why record a guide’s edition as well as its title?
cards.back: An identified version of a work, useful for determining which developments its account could include.

cards.front: What is the difference between a lead and a verified proposition?
cards.back: A lead points toward something to check. A verified proposition has been examined in the relevant source and still needs appropriate currency and applicability checks.

cards.front: Why are search words alone an incomplete query record?
cards.back: The request submitted to a collection, understood with its words, searched fields, syntax and active filters.

cards.front: How can a filter both help and hinder research?
cards.back: A restriction on a search collection, such as court, date, field or document type, which can focus results or exclude needed material.

cards.front: Why does the zero-hit title search not prove no room cases exist?
cards.back: IDX1 titles use Town Room Office. A full-text search for complete application returns Rowan, Cedar and Birch. Record the field and coverage of both queries.

cards.front: Why might a code section need additional enactment history?
cards.back: A subject-arranged section may omit the context needed to select an older version or apply a transition. Read the relevant enactments and amendment provisions before applying it to the event.

cards.front: What is a session law?
cards.back: An enacted law as published in the sequence of enactments, distinct from its later placement in a subject-arranged code.

cards.front: What three things should you check in an amendment?
cards.back: A legal change to existing text, whose exact scope, effective date and application must be read rather than inferred.

cards.front: How can enactment and effectiveness differ?
cards.back: A law can be enacted on one date but take effect later. Amendment A was enacted June 10 and takes effect July 1, with receipt on or after July 1 selecting its fourteen-day period.

cards.front: Why must a researcher read the transition provision before counting days?
cards.back: The transition provision selects which period applies before arithmetic begins. A1 preserves ten days for pre-July receipts even when their deadline falls in July.

cards.front: What does a delegation check ask about an agency rule?
cards.back: Ask what power the statute grants and what limits it imposes. Section 4 permits forms and identifying information but forbids extending the statutory decision period.

cards.front: Why is a regulation’s presence in a compilation insufficient by itself?
cards.back: Printed text can remain unchanged despite an adverse court decision. Compare the rule with its statutory authority and later treatment; Birch B2 rejects Rule 8.3’s fifteen-day proposition.

cards.front: What deadlines apply to Noor and Ivo under P4 and A1?
cards.back: Noor: June 25 receipt keeps ten days, ending July 5. Ivo: July 3 receipt gets fourteen days, ending July 17. Receipt is day zero.

cards.front: What does a case caption help identify, and what does it not settle?
cards.back: The identifying heading of a case, including named parties; it does not by itself establish the issue, procedural roles or result.

cards.front: Why read procedural posture before describing the result?
cards.back: It identifies the ruling under review and the court’s task. Birch reverses a timeliness ruling and remands; that does not establish a damages award or right to a room.

cards.front: Why identify an opinion’s type and speaker?
cards.back: The kind of judicial writing, such as majority, concurrence or dissent; identifying it helps determine whose position is expressed.

cards.front: How should a researcher identify the scope of a holding?
cards.back: A proposition decided as necessary to resolve the issue before the court; its scope requires reading the facts, task and reasoning.

cards.front: How does dictum differ from a holding?
cards.back: Judicial language beyond what is necessary to the decision; its classification and persuasive significance require context.

cards.front: Why must a search summary be checked against the opinion?
cards.back: A publisher’s description of an authority, which may aid discovery but is not the issuing court’s language merely because it accompanies the opinion.

cards.front: What does B2 add to a citation to Birch?
cards.back: B2 directs the reader to the specific passage that rejects the fifteen-day rule and overrules Cedar on that point, rather than requiring a search of the whole case.

cards.front: Which passage prevents reading Rowan as a decision about every electronic message?
cards.back: R3 expressly reserves unsavable messages. R2 accepts the supplied savable message under section 3; H1’s broader summary overstates that result.

cards.front: Why is an access date not a completed currency check?
cards.back: Access records when you opened a source. Currency requires examining later changes or treatment and stating the collection’s coverage; opening an August-15 index on August 20 does not extend it.

cards.front: What should follow a citator signal?
cards.back: Open the later authority and inspect the court, issue, reasoning and scope of treatment. Record the tool’s coverage; the signal alone does not establish the result.

cards.front: How does subsequent history differ from a separate case citing an opinion?
cards.back: Later proceedings in the same litigation, distinct from treatment of an authority by a separate later case.

cards.front: Why does negative treatment require proposition-level reading?
cards.back: Later authority that criticizes, limits, rejects or otherwise undermines an earlier proposition; the precise effect depends on the later text and authority.

cards.front: Why should updating focus on propositions rather than case names alone?
cards.back: Different propositions can receive different treatment. Birch B2 overrules Cedar’s timing point while B3 leaves Rowan’s message-form holding undisturbed.

cards.front: Which date limits what an updating index can establish?
cards.back: The date through which a collection or updating record states that its coverage extends.

cards.front: How should an unresolved research gap appear in the final handoff?
cards.back: Name the missing issue, period or collection, explain its effect on the conclusion, and specify a next action. Do not describe an unavailable search as completed.

cards.front: What remains open after reading the packet’s August records?
cards.back: Legislation and rule text are covered through August 20. The case index stops August 15, so later judicial developments for August 16–20 remain unchecked, as do materials outside its collection.

cards.front: What does jurisdiction identify when comparing Larch and Maren?
cards.back: In this course’s authority analysis, the relevant legal system; in other contexts the term also concerns a tribunal’s legal power.

cards.front: What makes authority binding in a stated forum?
cards.back: Authority the deciding forum must follow for the relevant proposition under the applicable hierarchy and other legal rules.

cards.front: What does persuasive authority permit without compelling?
cards.back: Authority that may inform reasoning without requiring the deciding forum to adopt the result.

cards.front: Why is “newest document wins” an inadequate hierarchy rule?
cards.back: Authority depends on the legal system’s hierarchy, the proposition and its applicability. A newer staff memo cannot override A1, and a newer Maren decision does not bind Larch.

cards.front: What does applicability check beyond source classification?
cards.back: The fit between a rule or version and the particular forum, issue, facts and relevant event date.

cards.front: What does authentication concern?
cards.back: Evidence that a document is what it purports to be and comes from the identified source, distinct from whether its law is current.

cards.front: Why can an unaltered old document still require updating?
cards.back: Whether content has been altered from the verified version; this does not establish the absence of later legal changes.

cards.front: Why do neither Elm nor M1 control the Larch transition?
cards.back: Elm applies a different jurisdiction’s twenty-day law. M1 is nonbinding staff guidance inconsistent with A1’s receipt-date rule. Identify both conflicts, not merely the documents’ dates.

cards.front: What must a useful citation let a reader do?
cards.back: A reference identifying a supporting source and directing the reader to relevant material under the applicable citation convention.

cards.front: Why distinguish H1’s editor from Rowan’s judges?
cards.back: H1 is editorial language, whereas R2–R3 state the judges’ decision and limits. Attributing H1’s broader words to the judges would misrepresent their holding.

cards.front: When can a short citation remain traceable?
cards.back: A shortened citation used after the source has been clearly identified, subject to the governing style and continuing clarity.

cards.front: What must be checked beyond the spelling of a quotation?
cards.back: Source language reproduced as such, with accurate wording, attribution and context preserved.

cards.front: Why does a paraphrase still need a citation?
cards.back: An attributed restatement of a source’s idea in new wording, still requiring support and an accurate representation of scope.

cards.front: When does shortening a quotation become misleading?
cards.back: When the shortening removes a condition or qualification that changes the source’s meaning. Dropping “savable” makes section 3 appear to answer a question Rowan R3 reserves.

cards.front: What does a bracketed alteration disclose?
cards.back: A visibly marked insertion or change inside quoted material when allowed by the applicable style, without distorting the source’s meaning.

cards.front: Which references support Noor’s retained ten-day period?
cards.back: Original Act section 2 supplies ten days; A1 preserves it for complete applications received before July 1, including Noor’s June 25 receipt.

cards.front: How does a research log differ from a list of links?
cards.back: A record of questions, source collections, queries, results, passages examined, conclusions and next actions during an investigation.

cards.front: What belongs in an authority table?
cards.back: An organized set of source entries showing propositions, status, versions, treatment and limits; labelled entries can serve the same function as rows.

cards.front: What makes a research trail auditable?
cards.back: A traceable record connecting research inputs, actions and conclusions so another person can inspect and reproduce the work.

cards.front: How should unavailable database or docket access be recorded?
cards.back: Identify the unavailable source or collection, the question it prevents you from resolving, and the next step needed. Record the check as unperformed, not merely “no results.”

cards.front: What is a useful stopping rule for a bounded assignment?
cards.back: Pause after resolving the assigned issues and contradictions within available sources, while documenting exact gaps and follow-up. Do not stop at agreement alone or pretend every uncertainty is closed.

cards.front: What makes a handoff more useful than “research more”?
cards.back: A transfer of findings, unresolved questions and concrete next actions so another researcher can continue the work.

cards.front: What does the portfolio rubric establish and what does it not establish?
cards.back: A learner’s review of work against stated criteria to guide revision; it is not external grading, credit or certification.

cards.front: What is the bounded capstone conclusion?
cards.back: Within the supplied authorities both decisions are late. Case-law coverage after August 15 remains open, no remedy is supplied, and silence does not approve an application under section 5.

references.title: Larch research packet — sources, versions and coverage
references.body:
# Original fictional research collection

All institutions, laws, cases, quotations, dates and search results below are invented.
They are not real authority. Year 4 and Year 5 are exercise years, not calendar years.
This collection is separate from the Alder cases in the previous course. Use only
this collection for scored exercises. Stable labels identify passages; no invented
reporter citation is presented as genuine.

## Assignment and authority rules

P1. Advise a student researcher preparing an educational memo for a fictional Larch
trial court. The topic is the deadline for the Town Room Office to send a written
decision on a complete application for a town-operated study room. The research
snapshot is August 20, Year 5. No actual filing or legal advice is involved.

P2. Larch's Supreme Court is its highest court. Its published majority holdings bind
Larch trial courts. Published Larch Court of Appeals holdings also bind those courts
unless displaced by the Supreme Court or applicable legislation. Maren is a different
jurisdiction; its decisions do not bind Larch courts. Primary source status alone
does not establish binding force. The packet supplies no federal issue.

P3. The statute controls over an inconsistent agency regulation. The agency may make
rules within the authority delegated by the statute. Agency staff memoranda are
nonbinding guidance. Commentary and editorial summaries are secondary sources.
These are stipulated exercise rules, not a complete account of real legal systems.

P4. Count calendar days with receipt as day zero. The next day is day one. June has
30 days; July and August have 31. No weekend, holiday, extension or service adjustment
applies in this packet. A complete application contains all items in Rule 8.1.
No other requirements or grounds for delay may be invented.

## Larch Community Study Rooms Act — original version

Publisher: fictional Larch Legislature. Enacted December 1, Year 3; effective
January 1, Year 4. Stable locator: Act, sections 1–5 (original version).

Section 1. This Act applies to applications to use a town-operated study room.

Section 2. The Town Room Office must send a written decision within ten calendar
days after receipt of a complete application.

Section 3. A written decision may be delivered on paper or in a savable electronic
message.

Section 4. The Office may prescribe application forms and required identifying
information by rule. A rule may not lengthen the decision period in section 2.

Section 5. Silence does not approve an application. This packet supplies no rule
specifying damages, judicial remedies, appeal deadlines or entitlement to a room.

## Amendment A — transition matters

Publisher: fictional Larch Legislature. Enacted June 10, Year 5. Effective July 1,
Year 5. Stable locator: Amendment A, sections A1–A2.

A1. In section 2, replace “ten” with “fourteen” for complete applications received
on or after July 1, Year 5. Applications received before July 1 remain governed by
the ten-day period, even when their decision deadline falls in July.

A2. Sections 1, 3, 4 and 5 are unchanged.

Register note AR1. The supplied legislative change register is complete for this
Act through August 20, Year 5. Amendment A is the only change recorded through that
date. This completeness stipulation covers legislation only, not judicial decisions.

## Rule 8 — agency regulation

Publisher: fictional Town Room Office. Issued December 15, Year 3; effective
January 1, Year 4. Stable locator: Rule 8, subsections 8.1–8.3.
The supplied rule register is complete through August 20, Year 5 and lists no amendment.

8.1. An application is complete when it states the applicant's name, the requested
room and the requested date of use.

8.2. For computing the decision period, receipt is day zero and the following day
is day one.

8.3. The Office may send its decision within fifteen calendar days after receipt
of a complete application.

The presence of 8.3 in this reproduced text is not proof that it remains legally
usable. Compare the statute and Birch below; the regulation has not been textually
removed from the packet's compilation.

## Rowan v. Town Room Office — Larch Supreme Court

Published majority opinion, February 2, Year 4. Stable paragraphs R1–R3.

R1. The Office received Rowan's complete application on January 5, Year 4. It sent
a savable electronic decision on January 14. The parties agree that the message
was delivered and that the application was complete. The trial court rejected the
message solely because it was electronic.

R2. Section 3 expressly permits a savable electronic message. This message meets
that requirement. The original section 2 uses a ten-calendar-day period. The
January 14 decision was sent within that period; the form objection fails.

R3. We reverse the trial court's form ruling. We do not decide what happens when
an agency sends a message that cannot be saved. We do not decide any remedy for
an untimely decision.

## Cedar v. Town Room Office — Larch Court of Appeals

Published majority opinion, November 8, Year 4. Stable paragraphs C1–C3.

C1. The Office sent Cedar a paper decision thirteen calendar days after receiving
a complete application. Cedar challenged its timeliness under section 2.

C2. We read Rule 8.3 as allowing fifteen days and treat the Office's decision as
timely. We therefore reject Cedar's timeliness argument.

C3. We affirm the trial court's timeliness ruling. This decision says nothing
about whether an electronic message qualifies as written.

## Birch v. Town Room Office — Larch Supreme Court

Published majority opinion, April 15, Year 5. Stable paragraphs B1–B4.

B1. Birch challenges a decision sent twelve calendar days after the Office received
a complete application. The trial court followed Cedar and treated it as timely.

B2. Sections 2 and 4 leave the Office no power to lengthen the ten-day period then
applicable. Rule 8.3 conflicts with those sections and cannot supply a fifteen-day
period. Cedar is overruled on that point.

B3. We reverse the timeliness ruling and remand. We do not alter Rowan's holding
about a savable electronic message. We do not decide a remedy for the late decision.

B4. This opinion addresses the original statutory text. Whether later legislation
changes the time allowed must be determined from that legislation and its
transition provisions.

## Elm v. Maren Study Office — Maren Supreme Court

Published majority opinion, June 1, Year 5. Stable paragraphs E1–E2.

E1. Maren's separate statute allows twenty calendar days for the application at
issue. The Office sent a decision after eighteen days, which is timely under that
statute.

E2. We apply Maren's twenty-day language. We express no view about Larch's statute.

## Nonbinding materials and leads

G1. Study Rooms Guide, edition January Year 5, page 4, by the fictional Larch Study
Clinic: “The Office has fifteen days to respond under Cedar.” This is commentary
published before Birch and Amendment A. The clinic is not a court or legislature.

G2. Study Rooms Guide, edition May Year 5, page 6, by the same clinic: “Birch rejects
the fifteen-day rule; consult sections 2 and 4 for the ten-day period.” This edition
postdates Birch but predates Amendment A. It links to B2 and the original Act.

M1. Office staff memo, June 20, Year 5, paragraph 1: “Use fourteen days for every
application still pending on July 1.” This nonbinding staff direction does not
accurately describe A1's receipt-date transition rule. Do not substitute it for A1.

H1. Editorial search summary attached to Rowan: “Electronic messages always satisfy
writing requirements.” This is a publisher's summary, not judicial language. Its
breadth exceeds R2–R3. The summary intentionally illustrates a research error.

## Searchable collection and treatment record

IDX1. The packet's case index covers published opinions of Larch's Supreme Court
and Court of Appeals through August 15, Year 5. It contains Rowan, Cedar and Birch.
A title search for “study room” has no hits because their captions use “Town Room
Office.” Searching full text for “complete application” returns all three. Searching
“Cedar” across full text returns Cedar and Birch. These are stipulated search
results for practicing a log, not a claim about any live search service.

IDX2. Treatment entries through August 15: Birch cites and overrules Cedar's
fifteen-day proposition (B2); Birch expressly leaves Rowan's electronic-message
holding undisturbed (B3). No other treatment is recorded in this supplied index.
It does not cover opinions issued August 16–20 or unpublished materials. Its
silence is not proof of no later treatment or completeness for other collections.

ACCESS1. For this exercise, no live database, paid citator or full court docket is
available. You cannot close the August 16–20 case-law gap from the packet. Record
it and describe the next search you would need. The legislative and rule-register
coverage in AR1 and the Rule 8 note does not fill that judicial coverage gap.

## Reading the packet responsibly

A successful answer identifies the best-supported result within these supplied
materials, distinguishes closed checks from open checks, and explains what remains
unverified. It does not assert that an invented case is “good law today,” promise
complete real-world research, or derive a remedy from a deadline alone.

references.title: Research workbench — plan, queries and authority entries
references.body:
## Start with a bounded question

Write the decision to be supported, forum, legal issue, relevant event dates,
research date, known facts, unknown facts and desired deliverable. Separate facts
from assumptions. Record what the available collection covers before searching.

For this packet: determine the decision period for a complete town-room application
under Larch law, as of August 20, Year 5, with case-index coverage only through
August 15. Distinguish the application receipt date from the eventual deadline.

## Query ladder

1. Start with the institution and problem: Town Room Office; application; decision.
2. Add variants: complete application; written decision; electronic message.
3. Search full text as well as titles, recording which field was used.
4. Follow citations to the Act, Rule 8, Rowan, Cedar and Birch.
5. Search for later citing material and legislative changes separately.
6. Reassess coverage and unresolved questions before stopping.

Use a platform's help for its exact search syntax. Quotation marks, connectors,
stemming and proximity functions do not behave identically everywhere. In the
packet, IDX1 supplies the search results; no software syntax is needed.

## Research log entry template

- Entry label and research date/time:
- Question being investigated:
- Source collection and coverage cutoff:
- Exact query or navigation path, including field and filters:
- Result count or specific result supplied:
- Document and passage opened; version and publisher:
- Proposition supported or rejected, with reasoning:
- Follow-up action; completion or unresolved limitation:

An unexecuted query belongs in a “planned next action” field. Do not list it as a
completed search. A query returning zero results still belongs in the log with its
coverage, because the zero means little without that scope.

## Authority entry template

Use labelled entries on a small screen; a spreadsheet may use the same fields as
columns. A filled entry is an authority-table row regardless of visual layout.

- Source identity and stable locator:
- Issuing institution; jurisdiction; source type:
- Proposition relevant to this issue:
- Authority in the stated forum, with the reason:
- Applicable version and event date:
- Later treatment or amendment checked:
- Coverage and unresolved limits:
- Intended use, or reason excluded:

Example: Cedar, C2 (Larch Court of Appeals, November 8, Year 4); published primary
judicial source; supports a fifteen-day period in its original text. Birch B2
subsequently overrules that proposition. Cite Cedar to explain history, not as the
current supporting rule for fifteen days. IDX2 covers treatment only through
August 15, Year 5; no claim of a completed real citator check is made.

## Stop and hand off

Stop when the assignment's necessary sources and contradictions have been examined,
remaining gaps are explicit, and another researcher can reproduce what you did.
A time budget can justify a bounded handoff; it cannot turn an incomplete check into
a completed one. Record the next source, the unresolved question and the consequence
of not answering it. Do not use the number of tabs opened as a quality measure.

references.title: Citation and currency — a working checklist
references.body:
## Course citation convention

These fictional teaching citations identify the source, issuing institution or
version, and exact passage. They are not a universal court citation style.
For real work, consult the assignment's instructions and the relevant court's
current rules and applicable citation guide.

- Case: Birch, B2 (Larch Supreme Court, April 15, Year 5).
- Original statute: Larch Community Study Rooms Act, section 2 (original version,
  effective January 1, Year 4).
- Amendment: Amendment A, section A1 (effective July 1, Year 5).
- Regulation: Rule 8, subsection 8.1 (effective January 1, Year 4).
- Commentary: Study Rooms Guide, May Year 5 edition, page 6 (G2).

In a document with a clear first citation, a short reference such as “Birch, B2”
may work for this exercise. A bare “page 2” cannot distinguish a case from a PDF
viewer page, and a broken link alone cannot identify a source. Preserve identity
and a stable locator even when also storing a URL or local filename.

## Quotation check

Read the original passage and surrounding qualifications. Compare every quoted
word, punctuation mark and omission with that version. Attribute language to the
right speaker. Use quotation marks for exact wording; cite paraphrases as well.
When brackets or ellipses are permitted by the applicable style, disclose changes
without altering meaning. Never remove a limiting word such as “savable” to make
an authority support a broader proposition.

Course example: Section 3 allows a “savable electronic message.” The phrase is
quoted from the invented Act. H1's broader editorial summary is not a substitute
for the statute or Rowan. The short quote does not establish whether a particular
message was delivered, retained or timely; those are separate questions.

## Updating by source type

Case: identify the deciding court, opinion type, proposition and later treatment;
open the later authority and read its scope. A negative treatment flag is a lead,
not a substitute for reading. A positive or absent flag is not a warranty.

Statute: identify the applicable version and event date; read amendments, effective
dates and transition provisions; record the update coverage. Enactment and effective
dates can differ. Do not assume the page accessed today governs an earlier event.

Regulation: check its text and amendments, statutory authority, effective date and
judicial treatment. A regulation can remain printed even when a court has rejected
its use for a particular proposition.

Secondary source: record author, edition/date, jurisdiction and references. Follow
its leads to primary sources and update those sources. An attractive explanation
or recent access date does not establish current authority.

## Four separate checks

- Identity: Is this the document and issuing body I think it is?
- Integrity: Has the copy been altered since its verified issuance?
- Currency: What changes and treatment have been checked, through which date?
- Applicability: Does this version and proposition govern this issue and forum?

An authentic old document may be outdated. A current foreign decision may not bind
the forum. A perfect citation may point to a passage that does not support the claim.

## Optional real-source orientation

These are navigation exercises, not prerequisites for the packet quizzes. Record
what you actually observe at the time you visit; page layouts and coverage change.

- [Office of the Law Revision Counsel — Currency and Updating](https://uscode.house.gov/currency.html): locate the currency information and classification tables, then inspect a chosen section's version and notes. Do not infer an effective date from the date you opened the page.
- [GPO — Authentication](https://www.govinfo.gov/about/authentication): distinguish authenticity and integrity evidence from a later-law check. Opening a PDF in a browser is not by itself evidence that a signature was validated.
- [eCFR — What is the eCFR?](https://www.ecfr.gov/reader-aids/understanding-the-ecfr/what-is-the-ecfr): read its legal-status explanation and verification directions before describing what the publication establishes.
- [Cornell Legal Information Institute — Basic Legal Citation](https://www.law.cornell.edu/citation/): compare the guide's approach with any applicable assignment or court rule. Do not invent a reporter volume or page number to complete a citation.

These official publisher explanations and the original citation guide were consulted
November 3, 2026 (America/Denver). Their contents are background for research method,
not evidence of current Larch law; Larch is entirely fictional.

references.title: Research portfolio — assignment, model and self-review rubric
references.body:
## The task

Research as of August 20, Year 5 for a fictional Larch trial court. Use the packet,
including all supplied update records. Prepare an authority table, a reproducible
research log and a 450–650-word explanatory note. The note must explain the applicable
deadline, rejected sources, currency checks and access limitations. This is an
educational exercise, not a filing or legal advice. No paid database is required.

File A: Noor's complete application for a town-operated study room was received
June 25, Year 5. The Office sent a savable electronic decision July 8. Delivery and
all completeness items are stipulated. The parties dispute only timeliness.

File B: Ivo's complete application was received July 3, Year 5. The Office sent a
paper decision July 18. Completeness and delivery are stipulated. The parties
dispute only timeliness.

P4 supplies all counting rules. Do not add holidays, extensions, retroactivity,
automatic approval, damages or a right to a room. No remedy rule is supplied.

## Portfolio contents

Use at least seven authority entries: original Act and Amendment A (separate entries),
Rule 8, Rowan, Cedar, Birch and Elm. Add the guide editions and M1 as evaluated leads.
Each entry should contain the fields in the Research workbench reference. Distinguish
source classification from its present use for a particular proposition.

Include at least six log entries: initial scope, a narrow query with zero results,
a revised query, following Cedar to Birch, checking Amendment A and its transition,
and a final coverage/gap assessment. IDX1 supplies the simulated search results.
Mark these as packet exercises; do not imply that you searched a live database.

Your note should answer both files and explain why the older fifteen-day rule,
M1's transition statement and Maren's twenty-day rule do not control. Include at
least one accurate quotation and precise passage locators for decisive propositions.
Do not claim an unperformed signature, citator or full-docket check.

## Worked model — compare after drafting

File A uses the original ten-day period. A1 chooses the application receipt date,
not the deadline date, and expressly preserves the old period for pre-July receipts.
June 25 is day zero; June 26–30 are days one through five; July 1–5 are days six
through ten. Deadline: July 5. July 8 is day thirteen, so the supplied authorities
support a late decision. Electronic form is separately permitted by section 3 and
Rowan R2; acceptable form does not make the decision timely.

File B uses fourteen days under A1 because receipt was July 3. July 4 is day one
and July 17 is day fourteen. The July 18 decision is day fifteen and late within
the supplied materials. Rule 8.3 supplies no valid extension: section 4 forbids
one and Birch B2 rejects the contrary fifteen-day proposition. A1 changes the
statutory period to fourteen, not fifteen.

Cedar remains a historical primary source but cannot support its overruled fifteen-day
rule. Birch B3 leaves Rowan's electronic-message holding undisturbed. Elm applies a
different jurisdiction's twenty-day statute. M1 conflicts with A1 by using the set
of pending applications instead of the date of receipt. The January guide predates
Birch; the May guide predates Amendment A. Both require primary-source follow-up.

A bounded conclusion is: “The supplied authorities support treating both decisions
as late. The legislative and rule registers cover August 20, but the supplied case
index ends August 15. I have not checked later judicial developments for August
16–20, unpublished materials or a full docket. A real matter would require those
checks as appropriate to its forum and issue. No remedy or automatic approval
follows from this packet; section 5 expressly rejects approval by silence.”

A model log entry: “Packet exercise, August 20, Year 5. Collection: IDX1, published
Larch Supreme Court and Court of Appeals opinions through August 15. Query: Cedar,
full text. Supplied hits: Cedar and Birch. Opened C2 and B2; Birch expressly overrules
the fifteen-day proposition. Follow-up: check post-August-15 decisions using a
current court collection or citator; unavailable under ACCESS1.” This records the
actual exercise and the unexecuted next step separately.

## Complete model portfolio — compare after your own attempt

This model is a packet exercise as of August 20, Year 5. It reports supplied search
results, not live searches. The following entries use labelled fields so they remain
readable on a phone. Their coverage statements apply only to the stipulated collections.
The explanatory note has its own word target; the table and log are separate.

### Authority entry 1 — original Act

Identity and source: Larch Community Study Rooms Act, sections 1–5; Larch Legislature;
primary legislation, effective January 1, Year 4. Proposition and use: section 2
provides ten days; section 3 permits a savable message; sections 4–5 limit agency
power and conclusions about relief. Status: governing statutory text under P3,
with A1 preserving ten days for Noor's June 25 receipt. Updating: read A1–A2 and
AR1 through August 20. Judicial coverage remains limited to IDX2 through August 15.

### Authority entry 2 — Amendment A

## Model explanatory note

This educational analysis addresses whether the Town Room Office sent timely written
decisions for Noor and Ivo in the fictional Larch trial-court setting. Both applications
were complete and their decisions delivered, as stipulated in files A and B. The
research snapshot is August 20, Year 5. The conclusions below are limited to the
supplied packet and its expressly stated coverage; they are not real-world legal advice.

Noor's June 25 receipt selects ten days. The original Larch Community Study Rooms Act,
section 2 (effective January 1, Year 4), supplies that period. Amendment A, A1 (effective
July 1, Year 5), preserves it for complete applications received before July 1 even
when their deadlines fall in July. Under P4 and Rule 8.2, June 25 is day zero. June
26–30 are days one through five, and July 1–5 are days six through ten. The deadline
is July 5; the July 8 decision, on day thirteen, is late within the supplied authorities.

Ivo's July 3 receipt selects fourteen days under A1. July 4 is day one and July 17 is
day fourteen. The July 18 decision is therefore one day late. Its paper form does not
extend the period. Likewise, Noor's electronic form is a separate issue from timeliness.
Section 3 permits a “savable electronic message,” and Rowan, R2–R3 (Larch Supreme Court,
February 2, Year 4), accepts the specified savable message while reserving other questions.
Noor's stipulated savable decision does not become timely merely because its form qualifies.

Rule 8.3's printed fifteen-day language does not authorize either delay. Section 4
forbids a regulation from lengthening the statutory period. Birch, B2–B4 (Larch Supreme
Court, April 15, Year 5), rejects that allowance and overrules Cedar's contrary point.
Birch addresses the original text; A1 supplies the later fourteen-day period while A2
leaves section 4 unchanged. Cedar, C2 (Larch Court of Appeals, November 8, Year 4), is
useful history but cannot support the displaced rule. Elm, E1–E2 (Maren Supreme Court,
June 1, Year 5), concerns another jurisdiction's twenty-day statute and does not bind
this forum under P2.

The guides and memo require similar care. G1 predates Birch; G2 incorporates Birch
but predates Amendment A. Their citations are research leads. M1's direction to give
fourteen days to every application pending July 1 conflicts with A1's receipt-date
boundary. Nonbinding staff guidance cannot replace that transition text under P3.

The legislative and rule-text registers cover August 20, but IDX1–IDX2 cover specified
published Larch decisions only through August 15. Judicial developments for August
16–20, unpublished materials and a full docket remain unchecked under ACCESS1. A
current court-collection or citator inquiry into the relevant propositions is a next
action, not a completed search. These limits prevent a claim of complete current-law
verification. Finally, lateness does not establish an award or automatic approval:
section 5 expressly rejects approval by silence and supplies no remedy rule. The
supported conclusion is that both decisions are late within the supplied authorities,
with the stated research limits preserved.
